lessons.title: 1.2 Zero-Shot, Few-Shot & Chain-of-Thought (CoT) Prompting Patterns
lessons.content:
### Engineering Reliable Reasoning with Few-Shot & Chain-of-Thought

Modern AI models respond dramatically better when given explicit structural patterns and intermediate reasoning steps.

#### 1. Zero-Shot vs. Few-Shot Prompting
- **Zero-Shot**: Asking the model to perform a task without prior examples. Best for straightforward summarization or translation.
- **Few-Shot**: Providing 2–5 high-quality input/output exemplars inside the prompt so the model learns the exact tone, schema, and edge-case handling required.

#### 2. Chain-of-Thought (CoT) Reasoning
When solving multi-step logic, math, or classification tasks, instructing the model to reason step-by-step before emitting its final answer reduces logic errors by over 40%.

```text
System: You are an expert AI Data Quality Auditor.
Task: Classify the user query intent and extract structured entities.
Instructions:
1. First, think step-by-step inside <reasoning> tags.
2. Verify all extracted values against the source text.
3. Output the final result strictly as valid JSON inside <output> tags.
```

#### Core Takeaways:
- Separate instructions, context data, and output format using clear delimiters (`###`, XML tags).
- Specify what the model should do when information is missing rather than letting it guess.

To reduce the number of input tokens billed

lessons.content:
### High-Precision Data Annotation & RLHF Evaluation

Every frontier AI model relies on human data annotators and domain specialists to align raw pre-trained models into helpful, honest, and harmless assistants.

#### The 4 Dimensions of Response Evaluation:
1. **Instruction Following**: Did the model obey every positive and negative constraint (e.g., word count, JSON format, forbidden words)?
2. **Factuality & Grounding**: Are all claims verifiable against the provided reference text, or did the model hallucinate unsupported facts?
3. **Completeness & Clarity**: Is the response thorough, well-structured, and easy to scan?
4. **Safety & Harmlessness**: Does the response appropriately refuse harmful requests while avoiding unnecessary preachy refusals on benign prompts?

#### Writing Golden SFT (Supervised Fine-Tuning) Responses:
When rewriting a suboptimal AI response during annotation, annotators craft a **Golden Response** that resolves all factual errors, removes filler phrases, and models ideal reasoning.

> **Orientation guide, course map, and pre-check (30 minutes total):**

> - **5 min:** Choose your audience person (Part C)

---

### Part A: Course Guide (5 min)

#### Welcome
Welcome, and thank you for joining. **AI Foundations** is a short, friendly course for anyone who wants to understand AI. You do not need any technical background, and you do not need to write code. By the end, you will be able to explain AI to someone else, and you will know how to use it more wisely.

#### What you will be able to do
- Explain what AI is, and tell AI, machine learning, deep learning, and generative AI apart.
- Describe in simple words how an AI system learns from data.
- Spot AI in everyday life, and name its benefits and risks.
- Explain what chatbots do well, where they go wrong, and how to check their answers.
- Make good decisions about when and how to use AI.

#### How the course works
The course takes about **7 hours and 20 minutes** (440 minutes). You can study at your own pace. Each part is short, so you can stop and start again when you like.

| Part | Time | What you do |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Orientation** | **30 min** | Read this guide, choose your audience person, check your tools, and take the pre-check |
| **Module 1: What Is AI?** | **50 min** | Read the lesson, sort everyday items in “AI or Not AI?”, and take a short quiz |
| **Module 2: How AI Learns** | **50 min** | Read the lesson and a short reading, do “Be the Algorithm”, and take a quiz |
| **Module 3: Generative AI and Chatbots** | **50 min** | Read the lesson and a short reading, do “Spot the Hallucination”, and take a quiz |
| **Module 4: AI in Society** | **50 min** | Read the lesson and a checklist, write “My Five Rules”, and take a quiz |
| **Guided lab** | **60 min** | Train a simple image classifier and test a chatbot |
| **“AI in My Life” assessment** | **120 min** | Audit five AI systems, test a chatbot, and explain AI to your audience person |
| **Reflection and review** | **30 min** | Reflect, retake the pre-check, and submit your work |

#### What you need
- A computer, tablet, or phone with a web browser and an internet connection.
- A webcam for the lab. If you do not have one, we provide a ready-made image set.
- Access to any chatbot for the lab and the assessment. Free tools are fine.
- A way to make a one-page infographic or a short written document.

#### How you earn your certificate and badge
- Take the four module quizzes. You can retake them, and each attempt has new questions (10 drawn from 20-question banks).
- Complete the **“AI in My Life”** assessment. Part of it is checked automatically, and part is graded with a rubric.
- Reach at least **70%** in both the automated part and the rubric part. Reach **90%** in both for a **certificate with distinction**.
- If you fall short, you can revise your work once, using the feedback.

#### Tips for success
- Study in short blocks, and take the activities seriously. They prepare you for the assessment.
- Use your own life for examples. The assessment uses the AI you already use.
- Try the tools, but always check important facts.
- Write the assessment in your own words.

#### Using AI in this course
You may use a chatbot to test it, to explore ideas, and to check your understanding. However, your audit, notes, explainer, and reflection must be in your own words. **Please never share passwords, bank details, ID numbers, or other private information with any tool.**

#### Help and access
All diagrams have alt text, and every activity has a text-only version. If you need extra help or a different format, contact the course team before you begin.

---

### Part B: Glossary Preview (5 min)
These ten words appear throughout the course. Read them now, and do not worry if some feel new. Each one is explained step by step in the modules.

| Word | Simple meaning |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Artificial intelligence (AI)** | Computer systems that do tasks that usually need human thinking |
| **Algorithm** | A set of steps a computer follows to solve a problem |
| **Data** | Information such as pictures, words, numbers, or sounds |
| **Model** | What an AI system has learned, saved as patterns it can use |
| **Training** | The process of studying examples to find patterns |
| **Prediction** | The model’s best guess about something new |
| **Machine learning** | AI that learns patterns from examples |
| **Generative AI** | AI that creates new content, such as text, images, or sound |
| **Hallucination** | A confident answer from an AI tool that is false or made up |
| **Bias** | An unfair or unbalanced tendency in results, often caused by the data |

---

### Part C: Choose Your Audience Person (5 min)
In the final assessment, you will explain AI to someone who does not know much about it. Choose that person now. This could be a friend, a relative, a neighbor, or a colleague. Choosing early helps you notice what is useful as you learn.

Record your answers in your **Personal Study Notes** tab below:
- **Who is your audience person?** *(first name or role is enough)*
- **What do they already know about AI?**
- **Why might they be curious or worried about AI?**
- **Write two questions they might ask you about AI.**

> **Privacy tip:** You do not need to use real names. A description such as *“my neighbor who is retired”* is fine.

---

### Part D: Tool Check & Confidence Baseline (5 min)
Check each item when you are ready:
- [ ] I can open this course on my device and read the lessons
- [ ] I have a webcam, or I will use the ready-made image set in the lab
- [ ] I can open a chatbot (free is fine), or I will ask for help with this before the lab
- [ ] I know how I will make my explainer: an infographic tool or a document
- [ ] I know where to ask for help or for a different format

#### Confidence rating (before you start)
Before you move to **Lesson 0.2 (Pre-Check)**, note your starting confidence (1 = not at all confident, 5 = very confident) in your **Personal Study Notes**:
1. *How confident are you that you could explain what AI is to a friend?* **My rating (1–5):** `____`
2. *How confident are you that you can check whether an AI answer is true?* **My rating (1–5):** `____`

You will track your **Before / After / Change** growth on your Pre-Check score and these two confidence ratings at the end of the course in **Segment 8**.

sections.title: Segment 2 — Module 1: What Is AI? (50 min)

lessons.title: 1.1 Written Lesson: What Is AI? (Rules vs. Learning, Map & 5 Myths)
lessons.summary: Say what AI is in simple words, compare rules vs. learning (21°C thermostat vs. spam filter), trace the story of AI (1950s–2020s), see the 4-term nested map, explore AI around you, and bust 5 common myths.
lessons.content:
> **What you will learn:** By the end of this lesson, you will be able to say what AI is in simple words. You will also see how AI, machine learning, deep learning, and generative AI fit together, and you will know which common ideas about AI are wrong.

---

### 1. What is AI?
First, let’s start with a simple idea. **Artificial intelligence (AI)** is a computer system that can do tasks that usually need human thinking. For example, it can recognize a face, understand speech, suggest a movie, or answer a question.

Notice that the word **“artificial”** means made by people, and **“intelligence”** means the ability to learn and solve problems. So, in other words, AI is a human-made tool that can learn from information and then use it to make a choice or give an answer.

However, AI is not a robot with feelings, and it is not magic. Instead, it is software. It follows math and patterns, and it works only with the information it has been given.

---

### 2. Rules versus learning: the big difference
Before we go further, we need to understand one key difference, because it explains almost everything in AI.

Imagine a **thermostat**. You set it to **21°C**. When the room is colder, it turns the heating on, and when the room is warm enough, it turns the heating off. This is a rule: *“If the temperature is below 21, then heat.”* A person wrote this rule, and the thermostat never changes it. As a result, the thermostat is **not really AI**.

Now imagine a **spam filter** in your email. Nobody can write a rule for every spam message, because spammers change their messages all the time. So, instead, the filter looks at thousands of examples of spam and normal email. Then it learns the patterns. After that, it can guess whether a new email is spam, even if it has never seen that exact message before. This is learning from examples, and it **is AI**.

> **In short:** **Rules:** a person writes the steps. **Learning:** the computer finds the steps by looking at examples.

---

### 3. A short story of AI
Next, let’s look at how AI developed. Don’t worry about memorizing dates. The story is what matters.
- **1950s — the idea begins:** First, scientists asked, *“Can machines think?”* In 1956, a group of researchers met and used the name *“artificial intelligence”* for the first time.
- **1960s to 1980s — rule-based systems:** Then, people built programs full of hand-written rules. For example, some programs helped doctors with medical questions. However, these systems were hard to update, because people had to write every rule themselves.
- **1990s to 2000s — machines start to learn:** After that, computers became faster and there was more digital data. Therefore, learning from examples became practical. This is the time when email spam filters and online recommendations began.
- **2010s — deep learning:** Later, new methods made computers much better at images, speech, and translation.
- **2020s — generative AI:** Finally, AI tools that can write text, create images, and hold a conversation became easy for everyone to use. That is why AI is in the news today.

So AI is not new. What is new is that it is now powerful and easy to use.

---

### 4. The AI family: four terms, one map
People use many AI words, and they often mix them up. Fortunately, the idea is simple. Think of circles inside circles, going from the biggest circle to the smallest:

| Layer (Outer to Inner) | Plain-Language Meaning |
| :--- | :--- |
| **ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE (AI)** *(Biggest Circle)* | Any computer system that does tasks that need human-like thinking. |
| **MACHINE LEARNING (ML)** *(Inside AI)* | AI that learns from examples instead of following only fixed rules (e.g., your spam filter). |
| **DEEP LEARNING** *(Inside ML)* | ML using many-layered **neural networks**, loosely inspired by the brain, great at pictures, sounds, and language. |
| **GENERATIVE AI** *(Smallest Circle)* | Creates new text, images, or sound—such as a paragraph, a picture, or a song. |

> **Diagram Alt Text:** *Four nested shaded boxes/circles going from largest to smallest: outer layer "Artificial Intelligence (AI): any computer system that does tasks that need human-like thinking," containing "Machine Learning (ML): AI that learns from examples," containing "Deep Learning: ML using many-layered neural networks," containing at the center "Generative AI: creates new text, images, or sound."*

**An easy way to remember:** Every generative AI tool is AI, but not every AI tool is generative AI. For instance, a spam filter is AI, but it does not create anything new—it only decides.

---

### 5. AI around you
Because AI is already in daily life, you probably use it every day:

| What you do | Where AI helps |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Use a map app** | It predicts traffic and chooses a faster route |
| **Watch videos or listen to music** | It suggests what you may like next |
| **Check your email** | It filters spam and suggests replies |
| **Unlock your phone with your face** | It recognizes your face |
| **Talk to a voice assistant** | It turns your speech into text and finds an answer |
| **Use a chatbot** | It writes, explains, or translates for you |

As you can see, AI is not only for scientists and big companies. It is part of ordinary life.

---

### 6. Myths about AI
Finally, let’s correct five common wrong ideas:

| Myth | Truth |
| :--- | :--- |
| **“AI is one single thing.”** | AI is a large group of different tools. A chess program, a face-unlock feature, and a chatbot are all AI, but they work in very different ways. |
| **“AI thinks and feels like a human.”** | AI finds patterns in data. It may sound friendly, but that does not mean it understands or feels anything. |
| **“AI is always right.”** | AI makes mistakes. Sometimes it gives a wrong answer in a very confident voice. That is why we always need to check important information. |
| **“AI will do everything by itself.”** | AI needs people to build it, give it data, and check its work. Because of this, people stay important. |
| **“You need to be a genius to use AI.”** | Many AI tools are made for everyday users. You can start with simple questions, and then you can learn more step by step. |

---

> **Key takeaways:**
> - AI is a human-made computer system that does tasks that normally need human thinking.
> - Rules are written by people. Learning means the computer finds patterns from examples.
> - The AI family has four levels: **AI → machine learning → deep learning → generative AI**.
> - AI is already in maps, email, phones, and entertainment.
> - AI is powerful but not perfect, and it does not think or feel like a human.

#### New words in this lesson
| Word | Meaning |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Artificial intelligence (AI)** | Computer systems that do tasks that usually need human thinking |
| **Algorithm** | A set of steps a computer follows to solve a problem |
| **Machine learning** | AI that learns patterns from examples |
| **Deep learning** | Machine learning that uses many-layered neural networks |
| **Neural network** | A computer model loosely inspired by the brain, made of connected layers |
| **Generative AI** | AI that creates new content, such as text, images, or sound |

lessons.content:
> **What you will learn:** How to tell the difference between fixed-rule automation and true data-driven AI across 10 everyday tools.

### Your Task (15 Minutes)
For each of the **10 items** below, decide whether it is **AI** or **Not AI** and note *why* in your **Personal Study Notes** tab before checking the Answer Key below.

1. **A pocket calculator**
2. **A fixed-rule thermostat** (turns heat on below 21°C, off above 21°C)
3. **An email spam filter**
4. **Video recommendations** (YouTube / Netflix)
5. **A voice assistant** (Siri / Alexa / Google Assistant)
6. **A washing machine timer**
7. **A spreadsheet `SUM` formula**
8. **Smartphone face unlock**
9. **A customer-support chatbot**
10. **A motion-activated grocery store door**

---

### Answer Key & Explanations
| # | Item | AI or Not AI? | Explanation |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **1** | **Pocket calculator** | **Not AI** | Follows fixed mathematical rules programmed by engineers; never learns from examples. |
| **2** | **Fixed-rule thermostat** | **Not AI** | Uses a simple `IF temp < 21°C THEN heat ON` rule written by a person with zero learning. |
| **3** | **Email spam filter** | **AI** | Uses Machine Learning trained on thousands of emails to spot changing scam patterns. |
| **4** | **Video recommendations** | **AI** | Learns from your watch history and millions of similar viewers to predict what you will click next. |
| **5** | **Voice assistant** | **AI** | Uses Deep Learning for speech recognition and natural-language understanding. |
| **6** | **Washing machine timer** | **Not AI** | Counts down fixed minutes and follows a preset mechanical or digital sequence. |
| **7** | **Spreadsheet `SUM` formula** | **Not AI** | Executes an exact arithmetic instruction on the cells you selected. |
| **8** | **Smartphone face unlock** | **AI** | Uses Deep Learning to recognize your unique facial geometry across different lighting and angles. |
| **9** | **Customer-support chatbot** | **AI** | Uses language models to interpret customer questions and generate helpful replies. |
| **10** | **Motion-activated grocery door** | **Not AI** | A simple sensor triggers `IF motion detected THEN open door`. |

lessons.title: 2.1 Written Lesson & Reading: How AI Learns + “Garbage In, Garbage Out”
lessons.summary: Learn the 4 steps of machine learning (data, training, model, prediction), the 3 learning types (supervised, unsupervised, reinforcement), and why data quality prevents bias.
lessons.content:
> **What you will learn:** By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain how a machine learning system learns from examples. You will know the four steps (**data, training, model, prediction**), and you will be able to name the three main ways machines learn.

---

### 1. Learning from examples
First, think about how a child learns what an apple is. Nobody gives the child a long list of rules, such as *“round, red or green, with a stem on top.”* Instead, you show the child many apples and say, *“This is an apple.”* After a while, the child can recognize an apple they have never seen before, even if it is a different color or size.

Machine learning works in a similar way. In other words, instead of writing rules for the computer, we show it many examples, and the computer finds the patterns by itself. This is why machine learning is so useful. Some problems, like recognizing a face or a spoken word, are too complicated for anyone to write down as rules.

---

### 2. The four steps: data, training, model, prediction
Every machine learning system follows the same four steps:

| Step | What happens | Spam example |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **1. DATA** | Examples are collected | Thousands of emails marked “spam” or “not spam” |
| **2. TRAINING** | The computer studies the examples to find patterns | The computer compares the spam emails with the normal ones |
| **3. MODEL** | The patterns it learned are saved | It saves patterns, such as pressure words, strange links, and requests for money |
| **4. PREDICTION** | The model makes a guess about something new | A new email arrives and is marked “probably spam” |

- **Step 1, Data:** Data is information, such as pictures, words, numbers, or sounds. The examples we use for learning are called **training data**.
- **Step 2, Training:** Next, the computer studies the training data again and again. Each time, it adjusts itself to make fewer mistakes. This process is called **training**.
- **Step 3, Model:** After training, what the computer has learned is saved as a **model**. You can think of the model as the “learned experience” of the system.
- **Step 4, Prediction:** Finally, we give the model something new, and it makes a **prediction**. For example, it says, *“This email is probably spam,”* or *“This photo shows a cat.”*

> **Remember:** The model is not a list of rules written by a person. It is a set of patterns that the computer found by itself.

---

### 3. Why predictions can be wrong
Because a model works with patterns, it makes a **best guess**, not a perfect answer. For instance, a spam filter may say an email is probably spam, but sometimes a normal email gets caught. Similarly, it may miss a new kind of spam that looks different from anything it has seen.

Therefore, we should never think of AI as always right. Instead, we should think of it as very good at patterns it has seen before, and less reliable when something is new or unusual.

---

### 4. Three ways machines learn
There is more than one way to teach a machine. Fortunately, the three main ways are easy to picture with everyday examples:

| Way of learning | Everyday picture | Example |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Supervised learning** | Studying with an answer key. Each example comes with the correct answer, called a **label** | A spam filter learns from emails labeled “spam” or “not spam.” A photo tool learns from pictures labeled “cat” or “dog” |
| **Unsupervised learning** | Sorting a box of mixed buttons into piles. Nobody tells you the piles, so you group the buttons by how they look | A shop groups customers with similar buying habits, without being told the groups in advance |
| **Reinforcement learning** | Training a dog with treats, or learning a video game by playing. You try something, get a reward or a penalty, and improve | A program learns to play a game by trying moves and earning points. A robot learns to walk by trial and error |

> **In short:** Supervised learning has answers, unsupervised learning finds groups, and reinforcement learning uses rewards.

---

### Part B: Reading (8 minutes) — “Garbage In, Garbage Out”
Computer experts have a short saying: **“garbage in, garbage out.”** It means that if the information we give a computer is poor, the results will be poor too. This idea is very important for AI, because a model is only as good as the data it learned from.

#### Three questions to ask about data
To judge whether data is good, we can ask three simple questions:
1. **Is there enough of it?** A child who has seen only one apple may not recognize a different apple. In the same way, a model with too few examples may not learn the pattern well.
2. **Is it correct?** If many photos in the training data have the wrong label, for instance dogs labeled as cats, the model will learn the wrong lesson.
3. **Does it cover everyone and everything?** This is called being **representative**. If the data leaves out some groups or situations, the model will not work well for them.

#### Example 1: The daylight camera
Imagine a model that learns to recognize street signs, but all of its training photos were taken on sunny days. As a result, it may work well at noon, but it may make many mistakes at night or in the rain. The problem is not the computer. The problem is that the data did not show those situations.

#### Example 2: Unfair results
Now imagine a face recognition tool trained mostly on photos of one group of people. Because the data was not representative, the tool will probably work worse for people from other groups. This kind of unfair result is called **bias**. Importantly, bias often does not come from bad intentions. It often comes from data that is incomplete or unbalanced.

Similarly, if a model learns from past decisions that were unfair, it can repeat those unfair patterns. This is why people must check the data and the results.

#### What can we do?
- Use data that is large, correct, and varied.
- Test the model on different groups and situations before using it.
- Keep a person in charge of important decisions, such as hiring or health.

> **In short:** Better data leads to better AI. Poor or unbalanced data leads to poor or unfair results.

---

> **Key takeaways:**
> - Machine learning means the computer finds patterns from examples instead of following only written rules.
> - The four steps are **data → training → model → prediction**.
> - A model makes best guesses, so it can be wrong, especially with new or unusual cases.
> - The three main ways to learn are **supervised**, **unsupervised**, and **reinforcement learning**.

#### New words in this lesson
| Word | Meaning |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Data** | Information such as pictures, words, numbers, or sounds |
| **Training data** | The examples a system learns from |
| **Label** | The correct answer attached to an example, such as “spam” or “cat” |
| **Training** | The process of studying examples to find patterns |
| **Model** | What the system has learned, saved as patterns it can use |
| **Prediction** | The model’s best guess about something new |
| **Supervised learning** | Learning from examples that come with correct answers |
| **Unsupervised learning** | Finding groups or patterns in data without answers |
| **Reinforcement learning** | Learning by trial and error with rewards |

lessons.title: 2.2 Activity: “Be the Algorithm” (Good vs. Narrow Training Data)
lessons.summary: Act like a machine learning system in two rounds: learn from 10 labeled emails, predict 5 new ones, then see how a narrow “FREE = spam” rule fails.
lessons.content:
> **Your goal:** Act like a machine learning system. You will learn from examples, make predictions, and then see what happens when the examples are poor. *(15 minutes total)*

---

### Round 1: Learn from good examples (7 minutes)
First, study these **10 labeled email subject lines**. This is your **training data**. Look for patterns.

| # | Subject line (training data) | Label |
| :---: | :--- | :--- |
| **1** | WIN a FREE prize now!!! | **Spam** |
| **2** | Claim your reward: click here today | **Spam** |
| **3** | Cheap pills, no prescription needed | **Spam** |
| **4** | You have been selected: send your bank details | **Spam** |
| **5** | Last chance: double your money in 24 hours | **Spam** |
| **6** | Meeting moved to 3 pm tomorrow | **Not spam** |
| **7** | Your library book is due Friday | **Not spam** |
| **8** | Photos from the weekend trip | **Not spam** |
| **9** | Invoice for October attached | **Not spam** |
| **10** | Can you review my draft report? | **Not spam** |

In your **Personal Study Notes**, write in one or two sentences: **What do the spam messages have in common?**

Next, predict the label for these **5 new messages**, and write the clue you used. These are your **predictions**:
1. *Urgent: verify your password at this link*
2. *Lunch on Thursday?*
3. *Congratulations! You won a free vacation*
4. *Notes from today’s class*
5. *Free parking available at the venue*

---

### Round 2: Learn from poor examples (8 minutes)
Now, imagine a different system. It was trained on a much narrower set of examples. In this set, every spam message contained the word **“FREE,”** and no normal message did. Because of this, the system learned only one pattern: **“FREE = spam.”**

Use **only that rule** and predict the labels for the same 5 messages again, then compare with Round 1:
1. *Urgent: verify your password at this link*
2. *Lunch on Thursday?*
3. *Congratulations! You won a free vacation*
4. *Notes from today’s class*
5. *Free parking available at the venue*

#### Think about it
- Which messages did the narrow system get wrong?
- Why did the narrow system make those mistakes?
- What kind of examples would you add to improve it?

---

### Answer Guide
| # | New message | Best label (Round 1) | “FREE = spam” result | Right? |
| :---: | :--- | :--- | :--- | :---: |
| **1** | Urgent: verify your password at this link | **Spam** | Not spam | **Wrong** |
| **2** | Lunch on Thursday? | **Not spam** | Not spam | **Right** |
| **3** | Congratulations! You won a free vacation | **Spam** | Spam | **Right** |
| **4** | Notes from today’s class | **Not spam** | Not spam | **Right** |
| **5** | Free parking available at the venue | **Not spam** | Spam | **Wrong** |

- **Round 1 pattern:** The spam messages use pressure and promises, such as “now,” “last chance,” “click here,” “prize,” and requests for money or private details. The normal messages are calm and about ordinary tasks. Message 5 is the tricky one: it contains “free,” but it is not spam. Learners who look at the whole meaning, not just one word, should get it right.
- **Round 2 lesson:** The narrow system missed message 1 because it did not contain “free,” and it wrongly blocked message 5 because it did. The problem was **poor and narrow data**, not a bad computer. Adding varied examples, including normal messages with “free” and spam without it, would improve the system.

lessons.title: 3.1 Written Lesson & Reading: Generative AI, Chatbots & The Verification Habit
lessons.summary: Learn how language models and image generators work, their 6 strengths and 5 limits (hallucinations, cutoff, bias, no understanding, privacy), and the 4-step Verification Habit.
lessons.content:
> **What you will learn:** By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain what generative AI does and how a chatbot writes its answers. You will know where it is strong, where it goes wrong, and why you should check what it tells you.

---

### 1. What is generative AI?
First, let’s remember the AI family from Module 1. Some AI tools recognize or sort things. For example, a spam filter decides whether an email is spam. In contrast, **generative AI** creates something new, such as a paragraph, a picture, a song, or a piece of computer code.

For example, you can type, *“Write a friendly message to invite my neighbors to a garden party,”* and a chatbot will write a new message for you. Similarly, you can describe a picture in words, and an image tool will draw it. This is why generative AI feels so different from older tools, and why so many people are talking about it.

---

### 2. How does a chatbot write its answers?
Now we come to the key question. How does a chatbot produce text that sounds so natural?

Think about the suggestions on your phone keyboard. When you type *“Good,”* the keyboard may suggest *“morning.”* It does this because, in the text it learned from, *“morning”* often follows *“Good.”* A chatbot works in a similar way, but on a much larger scale.

In other words, a chatbot is built on a **language model**. During training, the model studied huge amounts of text and learned which words and phrases usually go together. Then, when you send a request, called a **prompt**, the model builds its answer one small piece at a time. At each step, it predicts the most likely next piece.

> **Remember:** A chatbot is designed to write text that sounds right. It is not designed to guarantee that the text is true.

Because of this, a chatbot does not “look up” facts like a library catalog by default. Instead, it generates likely-sounding text from patterns. Some tools can also search the web, which can help. However, you should still check important answers.

---

### 3. How do image generators work?
Image tools follow a similar idea. During training, they studied very many pictures together with the words that describe them. As a result, they learned patterns that connect words and images. When you describe a picture, the tool creates a new image that fits those patterns. Notice that the image is newly made, not copied from a single photo, but it can still contain mistakes, such as strange hands or text that is spelled wrongly.

---

### 4. What generative AI does well
Generative AI is a useful helper for many everyday tasks. Here are some of its strengths:

| Task | How it helps |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Drafting** | Writes a first version of an email, letter, or post, which you then improve |
| **Summarizing** | Shortens a long text into the main points |
| **Translating** | Gives a quick translation that you can check or polish |
| **Brainstorming** | Suggests ideas, names, or approaches when you feel stuck |
| **Explaining** | Describes a hard idea in simpler words or with an example |
| **Practicing** | Acts as a partner for practicing a language or an interview |

In all of these tasks, the AI gives you a starting point. Then, you review and decide.

---

### 5. Where generative AI goes wrong
However, generative AI also has important limits. It is better to know them before you rely on it.

| Limit | What it means |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Hallucinations** | The AI gives an answer that sounds confident but is false or made up. For example, it may invent a book title, a statistic, or a web link that looks real but does not exist |
| **Outdated knowledge** | A model learned from information up to a certain date, called its **knowledge cutoff**. Unless the tool can search the web, it may not know about recent events |
| **Bias** | The model learned from human writing, which can be unbalanced or unfair. As a result, its answers can reflect those patterns |
| **No real understanding** | The AI finds patterns in language. It does not understand or feel like a person, even when it sounds friendly |
| **Privacy risks** | What you type may be stored or used by the tool, depending on its settings. Therefore, you should never share private information |

The most important limit for beginners is the **hallucination**, because the answer sounds correct. So the next reading teaches a simple habit for dealing with it.

---

### Part B: Reading (6 minutes) — The Verification Habit
Because AI can sound sure even when it is wrong, we need a habit that protects us. The habit has four steps. Fortunately, it only takes a few minutes.

1. **Step 1: Check it** — First, look at the answer and ask, *“What can be checked?”* Names, dates, numbers, quotes, and web links are easy to check. Be extra careful when the answer sounds very exact or very perfect.
2. **Step 2: Cross-check with a trusted source** — Next, look for the same fact in a trusted place. Good examples are official websites, well-known encyclopedias, and respected news organizations. If two independent trusted sources agree, you can feel more confident. If you cannot find the fact anywhere, treat it as unverified.
3. **Step 3: Ask for sources, then verify them** — Then, you can ask the chatbot, *“What sources can I check for this?”* However, do not stop there, because chatbots can invent sources. Therefore, open each link, or search for the title, and confirm that it exists and really says what the chatbot claimed.
4. **Step 4: Protect your privacy** — Finally, think about what you are typing. Never share passwords, bank details, ID numbers, private documents, or other people’s personal information. If you are not sure how a tool uses your data, check its privacy settings first.

#### How careful should I be?
| Situation | How much checking? |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Low stakes**, such as brainstorming party names | A quick look is enough |
| **Medium stakes**, such as a school or work document | Check every fact, name, and number |
| **High stakes**, such as health, money, law, or safety | Cross-check with trusted sources and ask a qualified person before acting |

> **Helpful prompt ideas:** *“Tell me if you are not sure.”* and *“Give me sources I can check.”* These can help, but they never replace your own checking.

---

> **Key takeaways:**
> - Generative AI creates new content, such as text, images, sound, and code.
> - A chatbot builds answers by predicting likely next words from patterns it learned.
> - It is useful for drafting, summarizing, translating, brainstorming, and explaining.
> - It can hallucinate, be outdated, show bias, and put your privacy at risk.
> - A confident answer is not always a correct answer, so check what matters.

#### New words in this lesson
| Word | Meaning |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Generative AI** | AI that creates new content, such as text, images, or sound |
| **Chatbot** | A program you talk to by typing or speaking |
| **Language model** | An AI model that learned patterns in language from large amounts of text |
| **Prompt** | The request or question you give to an AI tool |
| **Hallucination** | A confident answer that is false or made up |
| **Knowledge cutoff** | The date after which a model has not learned new information |
| **Bias** | An unfair or unbalanced tendency in results, often from the data |

lessons.title: 3.2 Activity: “Spot the Hallucination” (Eiffel Tower, Marie Curie & Pacific Ocean)
lessons.summary: Investigate three AI-written answers using the 4-step Verification Habit to catch the made-up claim hidden inside a confident answer.

> **Your goal:** Three AI-written answers are shown below. Two are accurate and one contains a made-up claim. Use the verification habit to find it. *(17 minutes total)* --- ### Step 1: Read (3 minutes) Read the three answers carefully. Underline or list any facts you could check, such as names, dates, and numbers. | Answer | Text (written by an AI chatbot) | | :---: | :--- | | **Answer A**
*(Eiffel Tower)* | The Eiffel Tower is in Paris, France. It was completed in 1889 for the World’s Fair, and it was designed by the engineering company of Gustave Eiffel. It was the tallest man-made structure in the world until 1930. | | **Answer B**
*(Marie Curie)* | Marie Curie was born in Warsaw, Poland. She won Nobel Prizes in both Physics and Chemistry, and she was the first person to win two Nobel Prizes. She also won a third Nobel Prize, in Medicine, in 1921. | | **Answer C**
*(Pacific Ocean)* | The Pacific Ocean is the largest and deepest ocean on Earth. Its deepest point is the Mariana Trench, which is about 11,000 meters deep. The Pacific covers roughly one third of the Earth’s surface. | --- ### Step 2: Investigate (8 minutes) Use a search engine or an online encyclopedia. For each answer, check the facts you underlined. Follow the verification habit: check, cross-check with at least one trusted source, and note where you found the information. ### Step 3: Record your findings (4 minutes) In your **Personal Study Notes**, record for Answers **A**, **B**, and **C**: - **Claim I checked** - **True or false?** - **Source I used** ### Step 4: Reflect (2 minutes) - Which answer contained the made-up claim, and how did you find it? - Why was it hard to notice by reading alone? - What will you do next time a chatbot gives you a fact? --- ### Answer Guide | Answer | Result | | :---: | :--- | | **A** | **Accurate.** The tower is in Paris, was completed in 1889 for the World’s Fair, and was designed by Gustave Eiffel’s company. It was the world’s tallest man-made structure until the Chrysler Building was completed in 1930. | | **B** | **Contains the made-up claim.** Marie Curie was born in Warsaw, won the Nobel Prize in Physics (1903) and in Chemistry (1911), and was the first person to win two Nobel Prizes. She did not win a third prize. The claim about a Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1921 is **invented**. | | **C** | **Accurate.** The Pacific is the largest and deepest ocean, the Mariana Trench is about 11,000 meters deep, and the Pacific covers roughly one third of the Earth’s surface. | > **Key lesson:** A hallucination can sit inside an answer that is mostly correct, and it sounds just as confident as the true parts.

sections.title: Segment 5 — Module 4: AI in Society (50 min)

lessons.title: 4.1 Written Lesson & Reading: AI in Society + The Responsible-Use Checklist
lessons.summary: Explore AI across 6 areas of life, 4 key benefits, 5 main risks (bias, privacy, deepfakes, energy, jobs), human-in-the-loop governance, and the Purpose-Data-Verify-Disclose-Human checklist.
lessons.content:
> **What you will learn:** By the end of this lesson, you will be able to name where AI is used in daily life and industry. You will also be able to weigh its benefits against its main risks, and you will know why people must stay in charge.

---

### 1. AI is already part of many areas of life
First, let’s look at the big picture. In earlier modules, you saw AI in maps, email, and phones. In fact, AI is now used in almost every area of society. The table below shows some examples, together with one thing to watch in each area:

| Area | How AI helps | What to watch |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Health** | Helps doctors notice patterns in scans and test results | Mistakes are possible, and health data is very private. A doctor should make the final decision |
| **Banking** | Spots unusual card activity to catch fraud, and helps check applications | Honest customers can be blocked by mistake, and decisions can be unfair |
| **Transport** | Predicts traffic, plans routes, and supports driver-assist features | Unusual situations can confuse the system, so safety checks matter |
| **Entertainment and social media** | Suggests videos, music, and posts you may like | You may see only more of the same, and you may spend more time than you planned |
| **Education** | Explains ideas, gives practice, and adapts exercises | Answers can be wrong, and copying can replace real learning |
| **Work** | Drafts text, summarizes meetings, and answers common customer questions | Quality still needs checking, and some tasks are changing |

---

### 2. The benefits
Because of these uses, AI brings real benefits. For example, it can **save time** on routine tasks. In addition, it can **find patterns** in large amounts of data that people would miss. Moreover, it can make things **easier to access**, such as automatic captions, translation, and reading text aloud. Finally, it can give **personal help**, such as practice questions that match your level.

---

### 3. The five main risks
However, AI also brings risks. It is better to know them early, so you can use AI wisely. Here are the five main ones:

1. **Risk 1: Bias and unfair results.** As you learned in Module 2, a model learns from data. If the data is incomplete or unbalanced, the results can be unfair to some people. For example, a system may work well for one group and badly for another.
2. **Risk 2: Privacy.** AI tools often need data, and some of that data is personal. Therefore, it is important to know what you share, who can see it, and how it may be used.
3. **Risk 3: Deepfakes and misinformation.** AI can now create very realistic fake pictures, voices, and videos, called **deepfakes**. As a result, something that looks or sounds real may be false. Whenever a clip or image shocks you, pause first. Then check whether trusted news sources report the same thing before you believe it or share it.
4. **Risk 4: Energy use.** Training and running large AI systems can use a lot of electricity. For this reason, it is wise to use AI when it helps, instead of using it for everything.
5. **Risk 5: Changes to jobs.** AI can do some tasks faster, so some jobs are changing. At the same time, new tasks and new jobs appear. Consequently, learning how to work with AI is a useful skill for almost everyone.

---

### 4. People stay in charge
So who is responsible when AI makes a mistake? The answer is simple: **people are.** AI is a tool, so the people and organizations that build it and use it must make sure it is safe, fair, and honest.

Experts call this idea **“human in the loop.”** It means that a person reviews and controls important decisions, such as hiring, health, or money. In addition, many places are creating rules for AI. For instance, the European Union has passed a law about AI. The details differ from place to place, but the goal is the same: to make AI safe and trustworthy.

---

### 5. Your role
Finally, remember that you are not only a user of AI. You are also a **decision maker**. You decide what to share, what to believe, and when to ask a human. The next reading gives you a simple checklist to help with these decisions.

---

### Part B: Reading (8 minutes) — The Responsible-Use Checklist
Whenever you use an AI tool, you can ask five simple questions. Together, they make a checklist that is easy to remember: **Purpose, Data, Verify, Disclose, Human**.

| Check | Ask yourself | Example |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Purpose** | Why am I using AI here? Is it a good fit for this task? | Using it to brainstorm ideas is a good fit. Using it to make a final medical choice is not |
| **Data** | What am I sharing? Would I be comfortable if it became public? | Never paste passwords, bank details, ID numbers, or other people’s private information |
| **Verify** | Have I checked the facts, names, numbers, and sources? | Cross-check with a trusted source before using a statistic |
| **Disclose** | Am I honest about using AI? What are the rules for this school or workplace? | If a course says to mention AI help, mention it. If it forbids AI, do not use it |
| **Human** | Who makes the final decision? Should a qualified person check this? | For health, money, law, or safety, ask a qualified person before acting |

#### Three short scenarios
Now, let’s test the checklist. Read each scenario and decide what you would do before checking the suggested answers:
- **Scenario 1:** A student asks a chatbot to write a whole essay and submits it as their own work.
- **Scenario 2:** An employee pastes a customer’s name, address, and phone number into a public chatbot to write a reply faster.
- **Scenario 3:** You receive a shocking video of a well-known person saying something unbelievable. Friends are already sharing it.

#### Suggested answers
- **Scenario 1:** The **Disclose** and **Purpose** checks fail. The student should follow the school’s rules, be honest about any AI help, and use AI to support learning, such as getting feedback, not to replace the work.
- **Scenario 2:** The **Data** check fails. Customer details are private. The employee should remove the personal details or use a tool that the company has approved.
- **Scenario 3:** The **Verify** check applies. Pause, look for the same story from trusted news sources, and do not share it until it is confirmed. It may be a deepfake.

> **In short:** **Purpose, Data, Verify, Disclose, Human.** A few seconds with this checklist can prevent many problems.

---

> **Key takeaways:**
> - AI is used in health, banking, transport, entertainment, education, and work.
> - The benefits are saving time, finding patterns, making things accessible, and personal help.
> - The five main risks are **bias**, **privacy**, **deepfakes and misinformation**, **energy use**, and **changes to jobs**.
> - People are responsible for AI, and important decisions need a **human in the loop**.
> - You can protect yourself with simple habits and a personal set of rules.

#### New words in this lesson
| Word | Meaning |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Deepfake** | A very realistic fake picture, voice, or video made with AI |
| **Misinformation** | False or misleading information, shared on purpose or by mistake |
| **Privacy** | Your right to control who can see and use your personal information |
| **Human in the loop** | A person reviews and controls important decisions made with AI |
| **Automation** | Using technology to do a task without a person doing every step |
| **Responsible use** | Using AI in ways that are safe, fair, and honest |

lessons.title: 4.2 Activity: “My Five Rules” + Where to Go Next
lessons.summary: Write five specific, realistic personal AI rules with reasons ("because"), test them on two real-world situations, and preview your next courses.
lessons.content:
> **Your goal:** Write five personal rules for using AI, one for each part of the checklist. Make them specific and honest, so you can really follow them. *(15 minutes total)*

---

### Step 1: Think (3 minutes)
Think about how you use AI now, or how you expect to use it. Which tools do you use? What do you ask them? What information do you share?

### Step 2: Write your rules (7 minutes)
Use the sentence frames below in your **Personal Study Notes**. Each rule needs two parts: **what you will do** and **why** (include *"because"*).

| # | Topic | Sentence frame |
| :---: | :--- | :--- |
| **1** | **Purpose** | *I will use AI for ___ and I will not use it for ___ because ___.* |
| **2** | **Data** | *I will never share ___ with an AI tool because ___.* |
| **3** | **Verify** | *Before I use a fact from AI, I will ___ because ___.* |
| **4** | **Disclose** | *When I use AI for ___, I will ___ because ___.* |
| **5** | **Human** | *For decisions about ___, I will ask ___ because ___.* |

### Step 3: Test your rules (3 minutes)
Next, check whether your rules would help in these two situations. Write one sentence for each:
- **Situation A:** You want a chatbot to summarize a long contract from your landlord. Which of your rules apply, and what will you do?
- **Situation B:** A friend sends you an audio clip of a famous person saying something shocking. Which of your rules apply, and what will you do?

### Step 4: Choose one to share (2 minutes)
Finally, pick the rule you think is most useful and imagine telling it to a friend or family member. Write it in one sentence.

---

### What good rules look like
| Topic | Weak rule | Stronger rule |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Data** | “I will be careful.” | “I will never paste passwords or private documents into a chatbot, because I do not know how the tool stores them.” |
| **Verify** | “I will check sometimes.” | “Before I use a number or a quote from AI, I will find it in a trusted source, because AI can invent facts.” |
| **Human** | “I will ask someone.” | “For health or money decisions, I will talk to a doctor or a bank adviser, because mistakes can be costly.” |

> **Self-check:** Strong rules are specific, realistic, and explain why (a sentence with *"because"*). Look at your weakest rule and make it more specific.

---

### Part F: Where to Go Next
Each course in the catalog is standalone, so you can choose whichever fits your goals after completing **AI Foundations**:

| If you want to… | Take this course |
| :--- | :--- |
| Get better results from chatbots and write stronger prompts | **Generative AI and Prompt Engineering** |
| Go deeper on bias, privacy, safety, and rules | **AI Ethics, Safety, and Responsible Use** |
| Save time at work or in study with AI tools | **AI for Productivity and Workflow Automation** |
| Understand how models are built and trained (coding) | **Machine Learning Essentials** |
| Design websites faster with AI help | **Web Design with AI** |
| Write and fix code with an AI assistant | **Coding with AI** |
| Add AI features to a website | **Integrating AI into Your Website** |
| Build an AI-powered application or solve a real problem | **Building AI-Powered Applications**, or the **AI Capstone** |

sections.title: Segment 6: Guided Lab (1.0h)

lessons.title: 5.1 Guided Lab Part A: Train & Test an Image Classifier (35 min)
lessons.summary: Teach a no-code image classifier 3 classes, test 6 new examples, break it on purpose with Narrow Data or Too Little Data, and record your observations.
lessons.implementation_tip: No webcam? Download our ready-made image set (Pen, Mug, Phone — 25 photos each + dim-light test folder) using the Upload option in Teachable Machine!
lessons.content:
> **Your goal:** Teach a computer to tell three things apart by showing it examples. Then, find out what happens when the examples are poor. This is the **data → training → model → prediction** flow from Module 2, and you will see it work. *(35 minutes)*

> **Privacy tip:** Use everyday objects or hand gestures. **Please do not use photos of other people’s faces.** Your images are for learning only, and you should not upload private photos. Check the tool’s privacy notice if you are not sure.

---

### Step 1: Set up (5 minutes)
1. Open the image tool in your browser (for example, [Google Teachable Machine](https://teachablemachine.withgoogle.com/)).
2. Choose an **Image Project**, and then the **Standard image model**.
3. Rename the first three classes. Choose three things that look clearly different. For example: *Pen, Mug, Phone*, or three hand gestures: *Thumbs up, Open hand, Fist*.
4. Write your three class names in the Step 6 observation table in your **Personal Study Notes**.

---

### Step 2: Collect training data (10 minutes)
1. For each class, record **20–30 samples** with your webcam. If you have no webcam, upload photos or use the ready-made image set from your course team.
2. Make the samples **varied**: change the angle, the distance, and the background a little each time.
3. Keep the three classes **balanced**, with about the same number of samples in each.

This is your **training data**. The **labels** are the class names that you gave.

---

### Step 3: Train the model (3 minutes)
1. Click **Train Model**.
2. Keep the tab open and visible until training finishes (switching tabs can stop it).
3. When it is done, you have a **model**.

---

### Step 4: Test it with new examples (5 minutes)
Now give the model something new. Show each object or gesture to the camera, or upload a new image. The model will make a **prediction**, and it will show how confident it is.

Run **at least 6 tests** (two for each class). Record the results in your **Personal Study Notes**, and **take one screenshot of the preview window while testing**:

| Test | What I showed | Model’s prediction | Confidence (%) | Right or wrong? |
| :---: | :--- | :--- | :---: | :---: |
| **1–6** | *(Record 2 tests per class)* | | | |

---

### Step 5: Break it on purpose (10 minutes)
Next, you will see what poor data does. Choose **one** of the two experiments:

- **Experiment 1: Narrow data**
  1. Delete all samples of one class.
  2. Record new samples for that class, but **all in the same conditions**: the same angle, the same light, and the same background. Make the other two classes different from this.
  3. Train again.
  4. Test again in normal conditions, with a different angle, light, and background.
- **Experiment 2: Too little data**
  1. Delete most samples of one class, so that **only 3–5 remain**.
  2. Train again.
  3. Test all three classes again.

Run **at least 6 tests** again, record the results in your **Personal Study Notes**, and **take one screenshot of the new results**.

---

### Step 6: Record your observations (2 minutes)
Complete these 5 prompts in your **Personal Study Notes**:
1. **My three classes were…**
2. **Number of right answers in Step 4 (out of 6):**
3. **Experiment I chose (1 or 2):**
4. **Number of right answers in Step 5 (out of 6):**
5. **What changed after I made the data poor?**

---

### Part D (Alternative for Part A if webcam/image tool is unavailable)
Two models were trained to tell apart a mug, a pen, and a phone. **Model 1** was trained on varied, balanced photos. **Model 2** was trained with all the mug photos taken in dim light from one angle:

| Test | What was shown | Model 1 prediction | Model 2 prediction | Notes |
| :---: | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **1** | Mug, bright light | Mug | Phone | Model 2 is wrong |
| **2** | Mug, dim light | Mug | Mug | Both right |
| **3** | Pen, bright light | Pen | Pen | Both right |
| **4** | Phone, bright light | Phone | Phone | Both right |
| **5** | Mug, side angle | Mug | Pen | Model 2 is wrong |
| **6** | Pen, dim light | Pen | Mug | Model 2 is wrong |

1. Count the correct answers for each model.
2. Explain why Model 2 made its mistakes. Which part of the data was the problem?
3. Describe two changes that would improve Model 2.

lessons.title: 5.2 Guided Lab Parts B & C: Probe a Chatbot, Debrief & Troubleshooting (25 min)
lessons.summary: Test a chatbot with a well-known fact, a tricky/obscure prompt, and a 3-source check; complete the 5-prompt debrief worksheet and save your evidence for the final assessment.
lessons.content:
> **Your goal:** Test a chatbot with three kinds of questions, check what it says using the 4-step Verification Habit from Module 3, and complete your Debrief Worksheet. **Keep your Part B screenshots and notes—you will reuse them in the final assessment!** *(25 minutes total: 20m Part B + 5m Part C)*

> **Before you start:** Do not type private information. Use general questions only. Chatbots can answer differently each time, so record what your chatbot really said, even if it differs from what others see.

---

### Part B: Probe a Chatbot (20 minutes)

#### Question 1: A well-known fact (3 minutes)
Ask something you can easily check, such as *“Who wrote the novel Pride and Prejudice?”* or *“At what temperature does water boil at sea level?”* Then check the answer.

#### Question 2: A tricky or obscure question (5 minutes)
Ask something that is hard or has a false idea inside it. Here are two examples you may use, or you may write your own:
- *“When did Marie Curie win her Nobel Prize in Literature?”* (Her prizes were not in literature, so does the chatbot notice?)
- *“Summarize the book ‘The Quiet River of Maplewood’ by A. Hartley.”* (This is a made-up title. Does the chatbot admit it does not know it?)

Then check whether the answer is **true**, **partly true**, or **invented**.

#### Question 3: A request for sources (8 minutes)
Ask the chatbot about a topic you know a little about, and then ask: **“Give me three sources I can check.”**
For each source, search for it. Does the page, article, or book really exist, and does it say what the chatbot claimed?

#### Record your results (4 minutes)
Take **one screenshot for each question** (3 screenshots total). Then complete these two tables in your **Personal Study Notes**:

| Question type | Question I asked | What I checked | Source I used | Result (correct, partly correct, or wrong) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **1. A well-known fact** | | | | |
| **2. A tricky or obscure question** | | | | |
| **3. A request for sources** | | | | |

For **Question 3**, list each source the chatbot gave:

| Source the chatbot gave | Does it exist? (yes or no) | Does it say what the chatbot claimed? |
| :--- | :---: | :--- |
| **Source 1** | | |
| **Source 2** | | |
| **Source 3** | | |

*(Alternative if no chatbot is available: Use the sample chatbot transcripts from your course team, mark verifiable claims, search for them, and fill in the tables above.)*

---

### Part C: Debrief and Submission (5 minutes)

#### Debrief worksheet
Answer each prompt in **two or three sentences** in your **Personal Study Notes**:
1. What did the image model learn from? Use the words **data**, **training**, and **model**.
2. What caused the model’s mistakes when the data was poor?
3. What surprised you in the chatbot test?
4. Which verification step was the most useful, and why?
5. What would you do differently next time you use a chatbot?

#### What to submit / Completion checklist
- [ ] Screenshot of the Step 4 test results
- [ ] Screenshot of the Step 5 test results
- [ ] Three chatbot screenshots, one for each question
- [ ] The tables in Part A and Part B, with every row filled in
- [ ] The debrief worksheet, with all five answers (at least two sentences each)

> **Keep your Part B evidence!** In the final **“AI in My Life”** assessment, you will build on it for the hallucination test, so save your screenshots and notes.

---

### Part E: Troubleshooting Guide
| Problem | What to try |
| :--- | :--- |
| **The webcam does not work** | Check that your browser has permission to use the camera. Or upload photos, or use the ready-made image set |
| **Training seems stuck** | Keep the tab open and visible. Wait one more minute, then refresh and try again with fewer samples |
| **The model gets everything wrong** | Check that each class has varied samples, and that the classes look clearly different from each other |
| **The model is right only for one class** | One class may have far more samples than the others. Try to balance them |
| **The chatbot refuses to answer** | Rephrase the question in a simple way. Do not ask for anything private or harmful |
| **The chatbot gives a different answer from a classmate** | This is normal. Record what your chatbot said, and check it |
| **I cannot find a source** | Treat it as unverified. Write “could not find it” in your table. That is a valid result |

lessons.content:
### Inside the Transformer: How LLMs Understand Context

At its core, a Large Language Model is a next-token prediction engine powered by the **Transformer** architecture.

#### 1. Tokenization
Before an LLM reads text, a tokenizer splits words into sub-word units called **tokens** (roughly 0.75 words per token in English).

#### 2. Semantic Embeddings
Each token is mapped to a dense numerical vector (an **embedding**). Words with similar meanings or context live close together in this vector space.

#### 3. The Self-Attention Mechanism
Self-attention allows every token in a sentence to dynamically weigh its relationship to every other token—resolving ambiguous pronouns, long-range dependencies, and complex syntax in parallel.

#### 4. Sampling Parameters (`temperature` & `top_p`)
- **`temperature = 0`**: Deterministic, greedy decoding—ideal for code, data extraction, and classification.
- **Higher `temperature` (0.7–1.0)**: Increases diversity and creativity for brainstorming and storytelling.

It compresses audio files into MP3 format
It replaces GPU memory with hard disk swap space
quiz_questions.explanation: Self-attention computes relevance scores between all pairs of tokens in the context window so the model understands context-dependent meaning.

### Decision Matrix: Prompting vs. RAG vs. Fine-Tuning

| Approach | Best Used When... | Key Advantage |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Prompt Engineering** | You need fast iteration on task formatting, reasoning, or tone | Zero training cost; immediate deployment |
| **RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation)** | The model needs access to up-to-date, private, or citeable documents | Eliminates knowledge cutoff limits & reduces hallucinations |
| **Fine-Tuning (SFT / LoRA)** | You need to teach a specialized style, domain vernacular, or compact model behavior | Lower inference latency with shorter prompts |

> **Welcome to Generative AI and Prompt Engineering — Orientation guide, course map, and pre-check (30 minutes):**
> - **5 min:** Read the course guide (Part A)
> - **5 min:** Preview the glossary (Part B)
> - **5 min:** Choose your real tasks (Part C)

---

### Part A: Course Guide (5 min)

#### Welcome
Welcome, and thank you for joining. This course teaches you how to get useful, reliable results from generative AI. You will learn to write clear prompts for **text, images, audio, and video**. You will also learn to check what AI gives you, use it honestly and safely, and build prompt templates that you can use again and again. You do not need any technical background, and you do not need to write code.

#### What you will be able to do
- Explain how prompts steer generative AI, and write clear prompts.
- Use techniques such as examples, step-by-step requests, roles, and prompt chaining.
- Prompt for images, audio, and video, and use pictures, charts, and documents as inputs.
- Use AI to study and research, while checking sources and keeping your own thinking.
- Check AI output for accuracy, bias, and fit, and improve your prompts from what goes wrong.
- Use AI media responsibly, with consent, honest labeling, and respect for privacy.
- Design workflows, and delegate multi-step tasks to AI assistants safely.

#### How the course works
The course takes about **15 hours**. You can study at your own pace, and each part is short. The course has **three parts**, and each part ends with a checkpoint where you can pause and come back later.

| Part and segment | Time | What you do |
| :--- | :---: | :--- |
| **Orientation** | **30 min** | Read this guide, choose your real tasks, check your tools, and take the pre-check |
| **Part 1: Text prompting — Modules 1–5** | **50 min each** | Prompting Basics, Prompting Techniques, Prompts for Real Work, Prompting for Learning and Research, and Checking and Improving Output |
| **Part 1 Checkpoint — Guided Lab 1** | **60 min** | Improve prompts, compare techniques, and test what breaks |
| **Part 2: Images, audio, and video — Modules 6–8** | **50 min each** | Prompting for Images, Audio and Speech, and Video and Multimodal Prompting |
| **Part 2 Checkpoint — Guided Lab 2** | **60 min** | Practice with images, audio, and video or multimodal inputs |
| **Part 3: Responsible and advanced use — Modules 9–11** | **50 min each** | Responsible Use Across Media, Advanced Workflows and Prompt Systems, and AI Assistants, Tools, and Agents |
| **“My Prompt Portfolio” assessment** | **170 min** | Complete five real tasks, check the results, and build reusable templates |
| **Reflection and review** | **30 min** | Reflect, retake the pre-check, and submit your work |

Every module has the same four steps: a written lesson, a short reading, a hands-on activity, and a quiz of 10 questions (drawn from a 20-question bank).

#### What you need
- A computer, tablet, or phone with a web browser and an internet connection.
- Access to at least one chatbot. A free version is fine.
- *Optional:* tools for images, audio, or video. These often have limits, accounts, or fees, and **you do not need to pay for anything**. Every task has an **analysis-only version** with sample outputs.
- A way to take screenshots, and a place to save your work.

#### How you earn your certificate and badge
- Take the quiz in each of the 11 modules. You can retake them, and each attempt has new questions.
- Complete the **“My Prompt Portfolio”** assessment. Part of it is checked automatically, and part is graded with a rubric.
- Reach at least **70%** in both the automated part and the rubric part. Reach **90%** in both for a **certificate with distinction**.
- If you fall short, you can revise your work once, using the feedback.

#### Tips for success
- Try every prompt yourself. Prompting is a skill that you learn by practicing.
- Keep a simple log of your prompts, the results, and what you changed. It makes your portfolio easier.
- Expect different results each time. AI tools do not always give the same answer, so record what you really got.
- Always check important facts before you use them.

#### Rules for using AI in this course
- You must use real tool output where tools are involved, but your **notes, reasons, playbook, and reflection must be in your own words**.
- Never share passwords, bank details, ID numbers, or other private information with any tool.
- Do not use a real person’s face or voice in your work without their permission. Use objects, places, made-up characters, or yourself instead.
- Label AI-made images, audio, and video as AI-made when you share them.

#### Help and access
All diagrams have alt text, and every activity has a text-only version. If you need extra help, cannot reach a tool, or need a different format, contact the course team. You will never lose credit because a tool is unavailable or costs money.

---

### Part B: Glossary Preview (5 min)
These ten words appear throughout the course. Do not worry if some feel new. Each one is explained step by step in the modules.

| Word | Simple meaning |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Prompt** | The request or instruction you give to an AI tool |
| **Output** | What the AI gives back, such as text, an image, or audio |
| **Context** | The background information that helps the AI understand your situation |
| **Format** | How you want the answer to look, such as a list, a table, or a short paragraph |
| **Iteration** | Improving a prompt step by step, based on the results |
| **Template** | A prompt with blanks that you can fill in and reuse |
| **Hallucination** | A confident answer from an AI tool that is false or made up |
| **Multimodal** | Able to work with more than one type of information, such as text and images |
| **Consent** | Permission from a person before you use their face, voice, or information |
| **Agent** | An AI tool that can carry out several steps on its own, such as searching and organizing |

---

### Part C: Choose Your Real Tasks (5 min)
In the final assessment, you will work on **five real tasks** from your own life or work. Thinking about them now will help you notice what is useful as you learn. Write down your ideas in your **Personal Study Notes** (you can change them later):

| **3. An audio or video task** | *(for example a voice script, a short clip, or a transcript)* |
| **4. A learning or research task** | *(for example understanding a topic or comparing options)* |
| **5. A workflow of at least three steps** | *(for example researching, writing, and making a picture)* |

> **Tip:** Choose tasks that do not need private information. For example, use a made-up business or a general topic if your real task is sensitive.

Tick each item when you are ready:
- [ ] I can open this course on my device and read the lessons
- [ ] I can open at least one chatbot, or I will ask for help with this before Module 1
- [ ] I know which image, audio, or video tools I can use, or I will use the analysis-only versions
- [ ] I know how to take screenshots and where I will save my work
- [ ] I know where to ask for help or for a different format

#### Confidence ratings (before you start)
Before taking **Lesson 0.2 (Pre-Check)**, record your starting confidence on a scale of **1** (not at all confident) to **5** (very confident) in your **Personal Study Notes**:
1. *How confident are you that you can write a prompt that gets a useful result?* **My rating (1–5):** `____`
2. *How confident are you that you can check whether AI output is correct and safe to use?* **My rating (1–5):** `____`

At the end of the course, you will retake the Pre-Check and compare **Before / After / Change** on your score (out of 10) and both confidence ratings.

lessons.summary: Learn why prompts shape AI output, the six-part checklist (T-C-A-F-L-E), vague vs. clear examples, common mistakes, and the "stranger test" reading.
lessons.content:
> **What you will learn:** By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain why prompts matter, and you will be able to write a clear prompt using a six-part checklist: **task, context, audience, format, limits, and example**. *(12 min lesson + 8 min reading)*

---

### Part A: The Lesson (12 minutes)

#### 1. What is a prompt, and why does it matter?
First, let’s start with the basics. A **prompt** is the request or instruction that you give to an AI tool. For example, you might type, *“Write a short thank-you note to my neighbor.”* The tool then gives you an **output**, which is the result, such as a piece of text, an image, or a sound.

Now, here is the key idea of this course. **The same AI tool can give very different results, depending on the prompt.** A clear prompt usually leads to a useful result, while a vague prompt usually leads to a generic or off-target result. In other words, you can get much more from the same tool by improving how you ask.

Why does this happen? As you may remember from earlier learning, generative AI works by predicting likely output from patterns. It does not know your situation, your goals, or your audience, unless you tell it. Therefore, when you give very little information, the tool has to guess, and its guesses are often average.

#### 2. A prompt is a brief
A helpful way to think about a prompt is as a **brief**. Imagine you give a task to a very capable new colleague who knows nothing about you. If you only say, *“Write something about our event,”* your colleague will have many questions. When will it happen? Who is it for? How long should it be? What tone do you want?

In the same way, an AI tool cannot ask you all these questions in the middle of a single prompt. Instead, it will fill in the gaps by itself. For this reason, a good prompt answers the most important questions before the tool starts.

#### 3. The six-part prompt checklist (T-C-A-F-L-E)
To make this easy, you can use a checklist with six parts. Each part answers one question that the AI would otherwise have to guess:

| Part | Question it answers | Example |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Task** | What do I want done? | “Write a welcome email.” |
| **Context** | What background should the AI know? | “for a new hiking club that meets on weekends in a city park” |
| **Audience** | Who will read or use the result? | “for adults who have never joined a club before” |
| **Format** | How should the answer look? | “about 100 words, with the three meeting times as a bullet list” |
| **Limits** | What should it include or avoid? | “friendly tone, no jargon, do not mention prices” |
| **Example** | Can I show what I like? | “Use a style like this: ‘Hi everyone! We’re so glad you’re here.’” |

> **Easy way to remember:** **T-C-A-F-L-E** — *Task, Context, Audience, Format, Limits, Example* — or simply “a brief that answers six questions.”

#### 4. Vague versus clear: two examples
**Example 1**
| Version | Prompt |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Vague** | “Write about dogs.” |
| **Clear** | “Write a 150-word friendly paragraph for a school newsletter about adopting a rescue dog. The readers are parents of young children. End with one tip for first-time dog owners. Use simple words.” |

The clear version names the **task** (write a paragraph), the **context** (a school newsletter), the **audience** (parents), the **format** (150 words, ending with a tip), and the **limits** (simple words).

**Example 2**
| Version | Prompt |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Vague** | “Help me with my email.” |
| **Clear** | “I wrote the email below to ask my landlord to fix a leaking tap. Please make it more polite and clear, but keep it under 120 words. Do not change the dates. Here is my draft: `[paste draft]`.” |

This time, the clear version tells the AI the situation, what to improve, what to keep, and the length. As a result, the output will fit the real need.

#### 5. Common mistakes
| Mistake | Quick fix |
| :--- | :--- |
| **The prompt is too vague** | Add the missing parts of the checklist, especially context and audience |
| **Too many tasks in one prompt** | Split the work into steps, and ask for one part at a time |
| **No context** | Tell the AI your situation in one or two sentences |
| **Accepting the first answer without checking** | Check facts, and improve the prompt if the result is not right |
| **Sharing private information** | Remove names, numbers, and private details before you paste anything |
| **Giving up after one try** | Treat the first result as a draft, and adjust the prompt |

#### 6. You do not always need all six parts
However, you do not need to write a long prompt every time. For a quick, low-stakes task, such as brainstorming party names, the task and the format may be enough. In contrast, for an important task, such as a job application letter, you should use all six parts and check the result carefully. So match the effort of your prompt to the importance of the task.

> **Remember:** Longer is not always better. A clear, relevant prompt beats a long, messy one.

#### Key takeaways
- A **prompt** is the request you give to an AI tool, and the **output** is what comes back.
- The same tool gives different results for different prompts, because the AI guesses what you did not say.
- Think of a prompt as a **brief** for a helpful new colleague.
- The six-part checklist is **task, context, audience, format, limits, and example**.
- Match the length of your prompt to the importance of the task, and always check important results.

#### New words in this lesson
| Word | Meaning |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Prompt** | The request or instruction you give to an AI tool |
| **Output** | What the AI gives back |
| **Context** | Background information that helps the AI understand your situation |
| **Audience** | The people who will read or use the result |
| **Format** | How you want the answer to look, such as length, list, or table |
| **Limits** | What the answer should include or avoid, such as tone or word count |

---

### Part B: Reading (8 minutes) — “A Prompt Is a Brief”
Imagine that you hire a helpful assistant on their first day. They are smart, fast, and eager, but they know nothing about you or your work. If you say, *“Make me a presentation,”* what will happen? Most likely, they will ask a lot of questions, or they will guess. If they guess, you may receive a presentation that is too long, too formal, or about the wrong topic.

An AI tool is similar. It is very capable, but it only knows what you tell it in your prompt. So the quality of your brief decides the quality of the result.

#### Four questions before you write
1. **What is the result for?** Say what you will use it for, such as a school newsletter, a work email, or a study guide.
2. **Who is it for?** The same message sounds very different for a child, a manager, or a friend.
3. **What should it look like?** Say the length, the structure, and the tone.
4. **What should it avoid?** Say what to leave out, such as jargon or certain topics.

#### The stranger test
Here is a simple test. Read your prompt and ask: **“Could a smart stranger do this task well, using only this prompt?”** If the answer is no, add the missing information.

| Version | Prompt |
| :--- | :--- |
| **First attempt** | “Write a speech for my sister’s wedding.” |
| **After the stranger test** | “Write a 2-minute wedding speech from me, the older brother, about my sister Anna. She loves hiking and is always late. Keep it warm and funny, not embarrassing, and end with a toast to Anna and her husband.” |

Notice that the second prompt gives real details, such as who is speaking, the length, the tone, and the ending. Therefore, the output will sound much more like the person who gives the speech.

#### A note on privacy
While you add details, be careful. Give the AI the information it needs, but **do not include passwords, bank details, ID numbers, or private information about other people**. You can use made-up names or general descriptions instead.

> **In short:** Write your prompt like a brief. Say what, why, who for, what it should look like, and what to avoid.
