| :--- | :--- |
| **Weak:** “Explain photosynthesis.” | Photosynthesis is the process by which plants, algae, and some bacteria convert light energy into chemical energy. It takes place in the chloroplasts, where chlorophyll absorbs light. Carbon dioxide and water are converted into glucose and oxygen through light-dependent reactions and the Calvin cycle. |
| **Clear:** “Explain photosynthesis to a 10-year-old in five short sentences, using a kitchen analogy. Then give me one question to check that I understood.” | Think of a plant leaf as a tiny kitchen. The ingredients are sunlight, water, and air. The plant mixes them to cook its own food, which is a sugar. While it cooks, it lets out oxygen, which we breathe. So plants are like chefs that run on sunshine. Check: What three ingredients does the plant leaf “kitchen” use? |

---

### Step 3: Think about it (2 minutes)
- Which checklist parts made the biggest difference?
- Which prompt was hardest to improve, and why?
- *For the text-only version:* Who is the weak output written for? Who is the clear output written for?

---

### Answer Guide and Feedback
There is no single correct answer. Here are sample strong rewrites so you can compare the level of detail:

| # | Sample strong rewrite |
| :---: | :--- |
| **1** | “Write a one-page report for my team leader on how our shop’s weekly sales changed in the last three months. The data is: `[paste numbers]`. Use short paragraphs and one table, in a neutral tone, and end with two suggestions.” |
| **2** | “Give me ten ideas for a low-cost birthday party for a 7-year-old who loves space. Put them in a list, with one sentence for each idea. The budget is 50 euros, and we have a small apartment.” |
| **3** | “Explain photosynthesis to a 10-year-old in five short sentences, using a kitchen analogy, and finish with one question to check understanding.” |
| **4** | “Here is my cover letter for a shop assistant job: `[paste text]`. Make it more confident and shorter, under 200 words. Keep my name and my work history unchanged, and do not add new facts.” |
| **5** | “Plan my week. I work Monday to Friday from 9 to 5, and I want to study 5 hours, exercise 3 times, and have two free evenings. Give me a table by day, with times, and keep Sunday free.” |

> **What good answers show:**
> - Each rewrite includes at least three checklist parts (such as task, context, audience, format, or limits) and is **at least 20 words**.
> - The rewrite gives enough detail that a stranger could do the task.
> - The rewrite avoids private information, and uses placeholders such as `[paste text]`.

---

### Stretch Task (Advanced Users)
Choose one of your improved prompts. Rewrite it **three times for three different audiences**, such as a child, a manager, and a close friend. Explain in one or two sentences how the changes would affect the result.

lessons.title: 1.3 Module 1 Knowledge Check (10 Questions from 20-Question Bank)
lessons.summary: Answer 10 questions randomly drawn from the 20-question Module 1 bank (15 minutes). Retake anytime for fresh questions with instant feedback.

quiz_questions.question: What is a prompt?
options: The request or instruction you give to an AI tool
The final answer from an AI tool
quiz_questions.explanation: A prompt is what you type or say to ask an AI tool for something.

quiz_questions.question: Which of these is NOT one of the six parts of the prompt checklist?
quiz_questions.explanation: The six parts are task, context, audience, format, limits, and example.

quiz_questions.question: In the checklist, “Format” answers which question?
options: How should the answer look, for example its length, a list, or a table?
quiz_questions.explanation: Format tells the AI how you want the answer to look.

quiz_questions.question: In the checklist, “Context” answers which question?
options: What background should the AI know about my situation?
What color should the answer be?
Which language is the tool written in?
quiz_questions.explanation: Context gives the AI the background it cannot guess.

quiz_questions.question: Which prompt is the clearest?
options: “Write a 150-word friendly paragraph for a school newsletter about adopting a rescue dog, with one tip for first-time owners.”
quiz_questions.explanation: The clear prompt includes the task, context, audience, format, and a limit.

quiz_questions.question: Why does a vague prompt often give a generic answer?
options: The AI has to guess what you want
quiz_questions.explanation: When you leave out details, the AI fills the gaps with average guesses.

quiz_questions.question: “A prompt is a brief” means…
options: Write it like instructions for a helpful new colleague who knows nothing about your situation
Always make it as short as possible
quiz_questions.explanation: A good brief gives someone everything they need to do the task.

quiz_questions.question: The prompt is “Write an email asking for a meeting.” Which parts would improve it most?
options: Context and audience, such as who it is for and why
quiz_questions.explanation: The AI does not know who the email is for or why you want to meet.

quiz_questions.question: Which is a good example of a “limit” in a prompt?
options: “Keep it under 100 words and avoid technical terms.”
quiz_questions.explanation: Limits say what to include or avoid, such as length, tone, or topics to leave out.

quiz_questions.question: Why might you add an example to your prompt?
options: It shows the style or format you want
It makes the AI slower on purpose
It replaces the need for a task
quiz_questions.explanation: Examples help the AI match the style you like.

quiz_questions.question: You ask for a recipe, a shopping list, a budget, and a travel plan in one prompt. What is the most likely problem?
options: The answers may be shallow or mixed up, so it is better to split the work into steps
The AI will refuse all of them
The AI will give perfect answers to all of them
quiz_questions.explanation: Too many tasks in one prompt often reduce quality. Ask for one part at a time.

quiz_questions.question: True or false: Every prompt must include all six parts of the checklist.
quiz_questions.explanation: Match the effort to the task. Quick tasks may need only the task and format, but important tasks need more.

quiz_questions.question: You are writing a job application letter. What is the best approach?
options: Use all six parts of the checklist, and check the result carefully
Accept the first answer without reading it
Share your passwords for more detail
quiz_questions.explanation: Important tasks deserve a clear, detailed prompt and a careful check.

quiz_questions.question: Which information should you leave out of a prompt?
options: A password or private ID number
quiz_questions.explanation: Private information may be stored or used by the tool, so keep it out.

quiz_questions.question: A chatbot gives a confident answer with a specific statistic. What is the best first step?
options: Believe it because it sounds exact
Check it with a trusted source
Ask the chatbot to repeat it
quiz_questions.explanation: AI can state wrong facts with confidence, so check important details.

quiz_questions.question: How does generative AI mainly produce its output?
options: By predicting likely output from patterns it learned
By looking up one correct answer in a book
quiz_questions.explanation: Because it predicts likely output, it does not guarantee that the output is true.

quiz_questions.question: The first answer is not what you wanted. What is the best next step?
options: Improve the prompt by adding what was missing, and try again
Make the same request again word for word
quiz_questions.explanation: Treat the first result as a draft, and adjust the prompt.

quiz_questions.question: Which prompt clearly includes an audience?
quiz_questions.explanation: Naming the audience helps the AI choose words and examples that fit.

quiz_questions.question: Which is a good “format” instruction?
options: “Give me a table with three columns: option, cost, and benefit.”
quiz_questions.explanation: A format instruction tells the AI exactly how the answer should be structured.

quiz_questions.question: True or false: A longer prompt is always better than a shorter one.
quiz_questions.explanation: Clear and relevant beats long and messy. Add the details that matter, and leave out the rest.

sections.title: Part 1 — Module 2: Prompting Techniques (50 min)

lessons.title: 2.1 Lesson & Reading: Five Prompting Techniques & “Ask It to Ask You” (20 min)
lessons.summary: Master giving examples, asking for steps, assigning a role, controlling format, and prompt chaining—plus using clarifying questions and specific conversational follow-ups.
lessons.content:
> **What you will learn:** By the end of this lesson, you will know five prompting techniques: **giving examples, asking for steps, assigning a role, controlling format, and prompt chaining**. You will also know when each one helps, and how to combine them. *(12 min lesson + 8 min reading)*

---

### Part A: The Lesson (12 minutes)

#### 1. Why learn techniques?
First, let’s connect this lesson to Module 1. There, you learned the six-part checklist, which helps you write a clear prompt. Now, you will learn **techniques**, which are ways of shaping a prompt to get better results for specific kinds of tasks. You can think of the checklist as your basic toolbox, and of the techniques as extra tools that you take out when the job needs them.

In this lesson, you will learn five techniques. Although they have different names, each one has the same goal: to tell the AI more clearly what a good result looks like.

#### 2. Technique 1: Give examples
Sometimes, it is hard to describe the style you want in words. In that case, it is easier to show it. When you include **one to three examples** in your prompt, the AI can copy the style, the tone, or the structure.

| Version | Prompt |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Without examples** | “Write a product description for a wooden desk lamp.” |
| **With examples** | “Write a product description for a wooden desk lamp in the same style as these two examples. Example 1: ‘Meet the Cozy Mug: it keeps your coffee warm and your mornings calm.’ Example 2: ‘Meet the Soft Sock: it hugs your feet and chases away cold floors.’ Keep it to one sentence.” |

- **Good for:** matching a tone or style, sorting items into groups, and repeating a format.
- **Tip:** Give more than one example, and make them a little different from each other. Otherwise, the AI may copy a single example too closely.
- **Tip:** Mark your examples clearly, for example with the word “Example,” so that the AI does not confuse them with the task.

#### 3. Technique 2: Ask for steps
Next, some tasks need careful thinking, such as comparing options, solving a problem, or making a plan. For these, you can ask the AI to work **step by step**. As a result, the answer is usually more organized, and it is easier for you to see where an idea came from.

| Version | Prompt |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Plain** | “Which phone plan is better, A or B?” |
| **With steps** | “Compare these two phone plans. First, list the price and data limit of each. Second, explain who each plan suits best. Third, put the main differences in a table. Finally, recommend one plan for someone who uses about 10 GB a month. Plan A: `[details]`. Plan B: `[details]`.” |

- **Good for:** comparisons, decisions, planning, and problems that have several parts.
- **Caution:** Steps that look logical can still contain mistakes. Therefore, read the reasoning, and check the numbers and facts yourself.

#### 4. Technique 3: Assign a role
In addition, you can tell the AI to take on a **role**, such as a patient tutor, a friendly editor, or a job interviewer. A role helps the AI choose the right tone, level, and focus.

| Version | Prompt |
| :--- | :--- |
| **No role** | “Help me prepare for a job interview.” |
| **With a role** | “Act as an interviewer for a shop assistant job. Ask me one question at a time. After each answer, give me short feedback and then ask the next question. Start with the first question.” |

- **Good for:** tutoring, practice, feedback, and writing in a specific voice.
- **Caution:** A role changes the style of the answer, but **it does not give the AI real qualifications**. If you say “act as a doctor,” the advice is not suddenly medical advice. For health, money, or law, always ask a qualified person.

#### 5. Technique 4: Control the format
Furthermore, you can tell the AI exactly how the answer should look. This is called **controlling the format**. You can ask for a table, a list, a certain length, headings, or a fill-in template.

| Version | Prompt |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Open** | “Give me a meal plan for the week.” |
| **Controlled** | “Give me a vegetarian meal plan for 7 days as a table with four columns: Day, Breakfast, Lunch, Dinner. Keep each meal to five words or fewer.” |

- **Good for:** results that you want to paste into a document or a spreadsheet, and for anything that you will compare or scan quickly.
- **Useful phrases:** *“in a table with columns…”*, *“in exactly three bullet points”*, *“under 100 words”*, *“in plain language”*, and *“with a heading for each part.”*

#### 6. Technique 5: Prompt chaining
Finally, a big task often works better as a **chain of smaller prompts**. In a chain, you ask for one step at a time, and you use the result of each step in the next one.

For example, imagine that you need to write a school report about renewable energy. Instead of asking for the whole report in one prompt, you can work in stages:

| Step | Prompt |
| :---: | :--- |
| **1** | “List the five questions a student should answer in a short report about renewable energy.” |
| **2** | “Using those questions, make an outline with three main sections.” |
| **3** | “Write the first section from the outline, in about 150 words, for a 14-year-old reader.” |
| **4** | “Suggest three ways to improve this section, but do not rewrite it yet.” |
| **5** | “Now apply my choice of improvements 1 and 3.” |

- **Good for:** long or complex tasks, such as reports, plans, and projects.
- **Why it works:** You control the direction, you can check each result before continuing, and it is easier to fix a small step than a huge answer.

#### 7. Choosing and combining techniques
| If your situation is… | Try this technique |
| :--- | :--- |
| **You want a certain style or tone** | Give examples |
| **You need to compare options or solve a problem** | Ask for steps |
| **You want practice, feedback, or a specific voice** | Assign a role |
| **You want to paste the result into a table or document** | Control the format |
| **The task is big and has several parts** | Use prompt chaining |

In many cases, you can combine techniques. For instance, you might ask a “friendly editor” (**role**) to improve your text in three steps (**steps**), and to give the result as a table of changes (**format**). However, do not add every technique to every prompt. Use only the ones that the task needs, because a clear, simple prompt often works best.

#### Key takeaways
- Techniques are extra tools that build on the six-part checklist.
- **Examples** show the style you want. **Steps** organize careful thinking. **Roles** set the tone and focus. **Format** controls how the answer looks. **Chaining** splits a big task into smaller prompts.
- A role changes style, not qualifications, and steps can still be wrong, so always check important results.
- Combine techniques when the task needs them, but keep the prompt as simple as possible.

#### New words in this lesson
| Word | Meaning |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Technique** | A way of shaping a prompt to get a better result for a certain kind of task |
| **Example** | A sample in your prompt that shows the style or format you want |
| **Step by step** | Asking the AI to work through a task in stages |
| **Role** | A character or job you ask the AI to take on, such as a tutor or an interviewer |
| **Prompt chaining** | Breaking a big task into a series of smaller prompts, where each result feeds the next |

---

### Part B: Reading (8 minutes) — “Ask It to Ask You”
So far, you have learned to tell the AI what you want. However, sometimes you do not know exactly what the AI needs to know. In that case, there is a simple trick: **let the AI ask you questions first.**

#### The clarifying-questions prompt
Add a short sentence at the end of your prompt, such as:
> *“Before you answer, ask me up to five questions that you need to do this well. Wait for my answers.”*

As a result, the AI will ask things like, *“Who is the audience?”* or *“How long should it be?”* Then, you answer, and the final result fits your needs much better. This is especially helpful when you are not sure which details matter.

| Speaker | Example |
| :--- | :--- |
| **You** | “I want a travel plan for a weekend in Lisbon. Before you answer, ask me up to five questions that you need to do this well.” |
| **AI** | “How many people are travelling? What is your budget? What do you enjoy: museums, food, walking, or nightlife? When are you travelling? Do you need accessible routes?” |
| **You** | “Two adults, about 300 euros, we love food and walking, in May, no accessibility needs.” |

#### Refine by conversation
You do not have to start again when the first answer is not perfect. Instead, refine it with short, specific follow-ups:
- *“Keep paragraphs 1 and 3. Make paragraph 2 shorter and simpler.”*
- *“Give me three different versions: formal, friendly, and very short.”*
- *“What is missing from this answer? What would you ask me to improve it?”*
- *“Explain the second point in simpler words.”*

Notice that each follow-up is specific. A vague follow-up, such as *“make it better,”* gives the AI very little to work with.

> **In short:** If you are unsure what to include, ask the AI to ask you. Then refine with specific follow-ups, instead of starting over.

lessons.title: 2.2 Activity: “Choose the Technique” & Stretch Comparison (15 min)
lessons.summary: Match six situations to the best prompting technique, test or compare outputs (live or text-only lamp descriptions), review sample prompts, and run a 2-technique Stretch comparison.
lessons.content:
> **Your goal:** Six situations are shown below. For each one, choose the best technique (or a combination), write a prompt, and explain your choice in one sentence. You can use a chatbot to test two of your prompts, or you can use the text-only version in Step 2. *(15 minutes)*

---

### Step 1: Choose, write, and explain (9 minutes)
Record your choices in your **Personal Study Notes** (make each prompt **at least 15 words**, using placeholders like `[details]` instead of private information):

| # | Situation |
| :---: | :--- |
| **1** | You want product descriptions in the same cheerful style as three descriptions you love |
| **2** | You must decide between two phone plans that have different prices and data limits |
| **3** | You want to practice for a job interview |
| **4** | You need a weekly meal plan that you can paste into a spreadsheet |
| **5** | You must write a five-page school report on a topic that you know little about |
| **6** | You want a travel plan, but you are not sure which details matter |

---

### Step 2: Test or compare (4 minutes)
- **Option A — With a chatbot:** Run two of your prompts. Record how well the technique worked, and what you would change.
- **Option B — Text-only version:** Read the two sample outputs below (written for this exercise; both answer *“Write a description for a wooden desk lamp”*) and answer the questions:

| Prompt | Sample output |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Without examples:** *“Write a description for a wooden desk lamp.”* | This wooden desk lamp combines natural materials with modern design. Its adjustable arm provides focused light for reading and working, while the warm wood finish complements any home office. |
| **With examples:** same request + two cheerful one-sentence examples (*“Meet the Cozy Mug…”*, *“Meet the Soft Sock…”*) | Meet the Wooden Lamp: it lights up your late-night reading and makes your desk feel like home. |

- Which output matches the cheerful style of the examples? Why?
- What did the examples change: the length, the tone, or the structure?

### Step 3: Think about it (2 minutes)
- Which situation needed more than one technique?
- Which technique would you use most often in your own life?

---

### Answer Guide and Feedback
| # | Best technique(s) | Sample prompt |
| :---: | :--- | :--- |
| **1** | **Give examples, and control the format** | “Write a one-sentence product description for a wooden desk lamp in the same cheerful style as these three examples: `[Example 1]` `[Example 2]` `[Example 3]`.” |
| **2** | **Ask for steps, and control the format** | “Compare these two phone plans. First list the price and data of each, then say who each suits, then put the differences in a table, and finally recommend one for someone who uses 10 GB a month. Plan A: `[details]`. Plan B: `[details]`.” |
| **3** | **Assign a role** | “Act as an interviewer for a shop assistant job. Ask me one question at a time, give short feedback after each answer, and then ask the next question.” |
| **4** | **Control the format** | “Make a 7-day vegetarian meal plan as a table with the columns Day, Breakfast, Lunch, and Dinner. Keep each meal to five words or fewer.” |
| **5** | **Prompt chaining** | Step 1: “List the five key questions a short report on `[topic]` should answer.” Step 2: “Make an outline with three sections.” Step 3: “Write section 1 in 150 words.” Continue one section at a time, and check each result. |
| **6** | **Ask it to ask you** | “I want a travel plan for a weekend in `[city]`. Before you answer, ask me up to five questions that you need to do this well.” |

> **What good answers show:**
> - The technique matches the situation, and you can explain why.
> - The prompt still includes Module 1 basics (task, audience, limits) and uses placeholders instead of private info.

---

### Stretch Task (Advanced Users)
Choose one real task. Run it with **two different techniques**, such as **examples** and **steps**. Write a short comparison of the results: which technique gave the better result, and why?

sections.title: Part 1 — Module 3: Prompts for Real Work (50 min)

lessons.title: 3.1 Lesson & Reading: Prompts for Real Work & “Your Prompt Library” (20 min)
lessons.summary: Apply prompting to 6 everyday text tasks, turn working prompts into reusable templates with [blanks], run the 5-point output check, and organize a starter Prompt Library.
lessons.content:
> **What you will learn:** By the end of this lesson, you will be able to use prompts for **six everyday tasks**, check the results before you rely on them, and turn a good prompt into a **reusable template with fill-in blanks**. *(12 min lesson + 8 min reading)*

---

### Part A: The Lesson (12 minutes)

#### 1. From techniques to real tasks
So far, you have learned how to write a clear prompt and how to use five techniques. Now, it is time to use these skills on real tasks. In this lesson, you will see **six everyday uses** of generative AI for text. Then, you will learn how to turn a prompt that works into a **template**, so that you never have to start from zero again.

#### 2. Six everyday uses
| Use | Example prompt | Be careful about |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Writing and editing** | “Rewrite this email to my landlord so that it is polite and clear, in under 120 words. Keep the dates unchanged: `[paste draft]`.” | Your own voice, and facts, names, and promises that the AI may change |
| **Summarizing** | “Summarize the text below in five bullet points for a busy manager. Keep every number exactly as written: `[paste text]`.” | Missing or distorted points, so compare with the original |
| **Explaining** | “Explain what inflation is to a 15-year-old, in four short sentences, with one everyday example.” | Mistakes in the explanation. You will practice checking in Module 4 |
| **Brainstorming** | “Give me 10 ideas for a low-cost fundraiser at a small school. List them with one sentence each, and avoid bake sales.” | Ordinary ideas. Treat them as starting points |
| **Planning** | “Make a 4-week study plan for a beginner’s Spanish exam. I have 5 hours per week. Put it in a table by week.” | Unrealistic times, costs, and dates. Check them against your real life |
| **Organizing information** | “Turn these messy notes into a table with the columns Task, Person, and Deadline. Keep every item: `[paste notes]`.” | Dropped or changed items, so compare with the original |

#### 3. A closer look: messy notes into a table
| Version | Prompt |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Weak** | “Make these notes better.” |
| **Clear** | “Turn the meeting notes below into a table with three columns: Task, Person, and Deadline. Keep every task, and do not invent deadlines. If a deadline is missing, write ‘not stated’. Notes: `[paste notes]`.” |

Notice the important details: the prompt tells the AI to keep every task, and says what to do when information is missing. Because of this, the AI is less likely to invent anything. Afterwards, you should still compare the table with your notes.

#### 4. From a good prompt to a template
A **template** is a prompt with blanks that you fill in each time. The fixed parts stay the same, while the blanks change:

| Part | Content |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Template** | “Write a `[length]`-word `[type of message]` to `[audience]` about `[topic]`. The tone should be `[tone]`. Include `[must-have points]`. Avoid `[things to avoid]`. Finish with `[ending]`.” |
| **Filled in** | “Write a 100-word update email to my team about the new printer. The tone should be friendly and brief. Include the date it starts and who to ask for help. Avoid technical words. Finish with a thank-you.” |

**How to build a good template:**
1. Start with a prompt that already works. Do not build a template from a prompt that gave poor results.
2. Replace details with blanks using square brackets, such as `[audience]` and `[topic]`, with short, clear names.
3. Keep the fixed parts (format, limits, tone).
4. Add a **“when to use it”** line (e.g., *“Use for short team updates”*).
5. Add one example if style matters.
6. Test it twice with different details, and improve it.

#### 5. Check before you use the result
In real work, the result is going to someone else. You are still the author, and you are responsible for it:

| Check | Ask yourself |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Facts** | Are the names, dates, numbers, and claims correct? |
| **Promises** | Did the AI promise something that I cannot or do not want to promise? |
| **Tone** | Does it sound like me, and does it suit the reader? |
| **Privacy** | Did I paste any private details that should not be there? |
| **Read aloud** | Does it sound natural when I read it out loud? |

#### 6. When not to rely on AI for real work
- The content is **private or sensitive**, such as customer details or health information.
- The task is an **important decision**, such as a legal, medical, or money decision, without a qualified person.
- You **need to learn the skill yourself**. If you let AI do all the work, you may not learn (Module 4 covers this).

> **Remember:** AI can speed up your work, but it does not take over your responsibility.

#### Key takeaways
- Six everyday uses are writing and editing, summarizing, explaining, brainstorming, planning, and organizing information.
- Each use has a typical risk, so check the result—especially names, numbers, dates, and promises.
- A template is a prompt with blanks that you can fill in and reuse.
- Build templates from prompts that already work, and test them with different details.
- Do not use AI for private content, or for important decisions without a qualified person.

#### New words in this lesson
| Word | Meaning |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Template** | A prompt with blanks that you can fill in and reuse |
| **Blank (placeholder)** | A part of a template written in brackets, such as `[audience]`, that you replace each time |
| **Draft** | A first version that you will review and improve |
| **Summary** | A shorter version of a text that keeps the main points |
| **Brainstorming** | Collecting many ideas, without judging them yet |

---

### Part B: Reading (8 minutes) — “Your Prompt Library”
A **prompt library** is simply a collection of your best prompts and templates (in a document, a notes app, or a spreadsheet) so you can find them quickly.

#### What to write for each entry
| Field | What to write |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Name** | A short name that starts with the task, such as *“Email: polite reminder”* |
| **When to use it** | One line, such as *“For gentle reminders to colleagues”* |
| **Template** | The prompt, with `[blanks]` |
| **Example** | One filled-in version, so that you remember how it works |
| **Notes** | What you learned, such as *“Works better when I give the audience”* |
| **Last improved** | The date, so that you know how fresh it is |

#### A small starter library
| Name | When to use it | Template |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Summary: meeting** | After a meeting, for people who were absent | “Summarize the notes below in `[number]` bullet points for `[audience]`. Keep every number exactly. Notes: `[paste notes]`.” |
| **Email: polite reminder** | For gentle reminders to colleagues | “Write a polite reminder to `[person]` about `[task]`, due on `[date]`. Keep it under `[length]` words and friendly.” |
| **Plan: study week** | When planning study time | “Make a `[number]`-day study plan for `[subject]`. I have `[hours]` hours per day. Put it in a table with columns Day, Topic, and Time.” |

#### Habits that keep a library useful
- **Keep it small:** Ten templates that you really use are better than a hundred that you never open.
- **Improve after use:** When a template gives a weak result, change it and note what you learned.
- **Review now and then:** Retire templates that no longer work, because tools and your needs change.
- **Keep private data out:** Never store passwords, customer details, or private information inside a template. Use blanks instead.

> **In short:** Save what works, name it clearly, and improve it over time.

lessons.title: 3.2 Activity: “Build a Template” & Stretch Instruction Set (15 min)
lessons.summary: Turn a repeated task into a reusable template with at least 3 bracketed blanks, test it on a second situation (live or text-only), and build a Stretch instruction set.
lessons.content:
> **Your goal:** Choose a task that you repeat, and turn a working prompt into a reusable template. If you have a chatbot, you can test it. If not, use the text-only test in Step 4. *(15 minutes)*

---

### A Worked Example
| Step | Result |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Task I repeat** | A weekly update email to my team |
| **Working prompt** | “Write a 120-word update email to my team about the new printer. The tone should be friendly and brief. Include the start date and who to ask for help. Avoid technical words. Finish with a thank-you.” |
| **Template** | “Write a `[length]`-word update email to `[audience]` about `[topic]`. The tone should be `[tone]`. Include `[must-have points]`. Avoid `[things to avoid]`. Finish with `[ending]`.” |
| **When to use it** | For short updates to a group of colleagues |
| **Test fill** | “Write an 80-word update email to my volunteers about the changed meeting room. The tone should be warm and clear. Include the new room number and time. Avoid long sentences. Finish with a welcome.” |

---

### Step 1: Choose a task (3 minutes)
Pick something that you really repeat: *thank-you messages, weekly updates, summaries of articles, social media posts, study plans, or reminder emails*.

### Step 2: Write a working prompt (4 minutes)
Write one clear prompt for a real or made-up situation, using the Module 1 checklist and, if useful, a technique from Module 2. Use made-up details if the real ones are private.

### Step 3: Turn it into a template (5 minutes)
Replace the specific details with **at least three blanks** in square brackets (`[...]`). Keep the fixed instructions for format, limits, and tone. Add a **“when to use it”** line, and record all 5 fields in your **Personal Study Notes**:
- **The task I repeat**
- **My working prompt**
- **My template (at least 3 blanks)**
- **When to use it**
- **Test fill (a different situation)**

### Step 4: Test it (3 minutes)
- **Option A — With a chatbot:** Fill the blanks for a different situation, and run the prompt. Does the result fit what you wanted? If not, change the template.
- **Option B — Text-only version:** Fill the blanks again with different details, and read the new prompt carefully. Ask yourself: *Is anything unclear? Is any blank missing? Would the result fit the new situation?* Make one improvement to your template.

---

### Answer Guide and Feedback
| Task | Sample template |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Thank-you message** | “Write a `[length]`-word thank-you message to `[person]` for `[reason]`. The tone should be `[tone]`. Mention `[one detail]`. Avoid `[things to avoid]`. Finish with `[ending]`.” *When to use it:* for short, personal thanks. |
| **Article summary** | “Summarize the text below in `[number]` bullet points for `[audience]`. Keep every number and name exactly as written. If something is unclear, say so. Text: `[paste text]`.” *When to use it:* for quick summaries of articles or reports. |

> **What good answers show:** At least three clear blanks with short, meaningful names; fixed parts for format, limits, or tone; a “when to use it” line; and zero private information inside the template.

---

### Stretch Task (Advanced Users)
Write a **short instruction set** that makes the AI always answer in the same structure—for example: *“Always answer with three parts: Summary (one sentence), Key points (three bullets), and Next step (one sentence).”* Test it on two different topics.

sections.title: Part 1 — Module 4: Prompting for Learning and Research (50 min)

lessons.title: 4.1 Lesson & Reading: Prompting for Learning and Research & “Ask It to Teach, Not to Answer” (20 min)
lessons.summary: Use AI as a tutor and practice partner, follow a simple five-step research workflow, check suggested sources, spot one-sided answers, and keep your own thinking in charge.
lessons.content:
**COURSE 2 | PART 1: TEXT PROMPTING**
**Module 4: Prompting for Learning and Research**
*Written lesson and reading (20 minutes)*

| Item | Details |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Module time** | 50 minutes: written lesson (12 min), reading (8 min), activity (15 min), knowledge check (15 min) |
| **Level** | Beginner to Intermediate. Modules 1 to 3 are helpful |
| **Tools** | A chatbot and a web browser are helpful for the activity. A text-only version is included |
| **Format** | Written lesson with tables, a short reading, a study-and-source-checking activity, and a quiz |

---

### Part A: The Lesson (12 minutes)

> **What you will learn:** By the end of this lesson, you will be able to use AI as a tutor and a practice partner, follow a simple five-step research workflow, check the sources that AI gives you, and keep your own thinking in charge.

#### 1. Learning is not the same as finishing
First, let’s think about the goal. When you use AI for study or research, you can use it in two very different ways. In the first way, you let it do the work, so that you finish faster. In the second way, you use it to understand the material better. Both can save time. However, only the second way helps you to learn.

Therefore, in this lesson, the goal is simple: to use AI so that you know and understand more, while you also stay honest and check what the AI says.

#### 2. AI as a tutor
A good tutor explains things at your level, gives examples, and answers your questions patiently. Generative AI can do something similar. For instance, you can try prompts like these:
- “Explain how solar panels work to a beginner, in five short sentences.”
- “Explain it again, using an everyday comparison.”
- “What are three mistakes that beginners often make with this topic?”
- “I am a 15-year-old with no science background. Which words should I learn first?”

However, remember that a tutor can make mistakes. So, when an explanation matters, compare it with your textbook, your teacher, or another trusted source.

#### 3. AI as a practice partner
Next, AI can help you practice. Practicing is often more useful than rereading, because it shows what you really understand. Here are three ways to do it.

| Way to practice | Example prompt |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Quiz me** | “Quiz me on solar panels with five questions, one at a time. Wait for my answer, tell me whether it is right, and explain briefly.” |
| **Teach-back** | “I will explain how solar panels work in my own words. Tell me what is missing or wrong, but do not give me the full answer first. Here is my explanation: [your explanation].” |
| **Flashcards** | “Make ten flashcards about solar panels with a question on one side and a short answer on the other.” |

Notice that in the first two examples, you do the thinking, and the AI gives feedback. This is a much better way to learn than asking for answers.

#### 4. A simple research workflow
Now, let’s move from studying to research. Research means finding out about a question, using several sources. A simple workflow has five steps, and AI can help with each one, as long as you stay in charge.

| Step | How AI can help | Your job |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **1. Define the question** | Helps you make a broad topic into a clear question | Decide what you really want to know |
| **2. Gather sources** | Suggests where to look and what words to search for | Find and open the real sources yourself |
| **3. Summarize each source** | Summarizes the text that you paste in | Read the source, and compare the summary with it |
| **4. Compare views** | Lists where sources agree and differ | Check that the comparison is fair and complete |
| **5. Write your conclusion** | Gives feedback on your draft | Write the conclusion yourself, in your own words |

#### 5. Sources: find them, open them, check them
The most important rule in research with AI is this: **a source is only a source if you can find and open it.** As you learned in earlier modules, chatbots can invent sources. They may give you an author, a title, a year, and even a web address, and still none of it is real.

So, whenever AI suggests a source, follow these steps:
1. **Find it.** Search for the exact title, or go to the organization’s own website.
2. **Open it.** Check that it exists, and read the relevant part.
3. **Check it.** Does it really say what the AI claimed? Who wrote it, and when? Is the author or organization trustworthy?

If you cannot find it, do not use it. Write “unverified” in your notes.

> **A useful trick:** Instead of asking the AI to recall facts from memory, paste the real text of a source, and ask the AI to summarize or explain that text. The answer is then based on something that you can check.

#### 6. Missing viewpoints and one-sided answers
In addition, an AI answer can sound complete and still be one-sided. For example, it might only mention one opinion, or it might leave out evidence that does not fit. To find out, ask questions such as:
- “What would someone who disagrees say?”
- “What evidence or viewpoints are missing from this answer?”
- “What are the strongest arguments on each side?”

Then, check the answers against real sources, because the AI’s counter-arguments can contain mistakes too.

#### 7. Keep your own thinking in charge
Finally, there is a risk called **over-reliance**. This means depending on AI so much that you stop thinking for yourself. If you always ask AI for the answer, you may finish quickly, but you may not remember or understand anything later.
- **Try first.** Make your own attempt, and then ask AI for a hint or feedback.
- **Write your own conclusions.** Use AI to improve your work, not to replace your thinking.
- **Be honest.** Follow the rules of your school or workplace, and say how you used AI when you are asked to.

#### Key takeaways
- Use AI to understand, not only to finish. Practice with quizzes and teach-back.
- The five research steps are: define the question, gather sources, summarize each source, compare views, and write your own conclusion.
- Find and open every source that AI suggests. If you cannot find it, do not use it.
- Ask for missing viewpoints, and check the answers against real sources.
- Avoid over-reliance, write your own conclusions, and be honest about AI help.

#### New words in this lesson
| Word | Meaning |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Tutor** | Someone or something that explains a topic and helps you learn it |
| **Teach-back** | Explaining a topic in your own words, and asking for feedback on what is missing or wrong |
| **Source** | A real document, page, book, or data that information comes from |
| **Verify** | To check that something is true, or that a source really exists and says what is claimed |
| **Over-reliance** | Depending on AI so much that you stop thinking and learning for yourself |
| **Perspective** | A viewpoint or way of looking at a question |

---

### Part B: Reading (8 minutes): “Ask It to Teach, Not to Answer”

Imagine two students who both use AI to prepare for a test. The first student types every homework question into a chatbot and copies the answers. The second student tries each question first, and then uses the chatbot to check the work and to get hints. On the test day, which student is better prepared?

Most teachers and learners would say the second student. When you make an effort yourself, even if it is a small one, you usually remember more. So the best way to use AI for learning is to ask it to teach, not just to answer.

#### The hint ladder
One helpful method is the **hint ladder**. You start with the smallest help, and you only go up one step when you are really stuck.

| Step | What you ask |
| :--- | :--- |
| **1** | “Do not solve it. Ask me one question that helps me start.” |
| **2** | “Give me a small hint about the next step, without the answer.” |
| **3** | “Show me a similar example, and let me try the real one myself.” |
| **4** | “Now explain the full solution step by step, and tell me what I misunderstood.” |

#### Prompts that make AI teach
- “Act as a patient tutor. Do not give the final answer. Ask me guiding questions.”
- “Check my work and tell me where I made a mistake, but let me fix it myself.”
- “After I answer, tell me what I got right, what I got wrong, and why.”
- “Explain this in a different way, because I did not understand the first explanation.”

#### Two cautions
1. **The tutor can be wrong.** If a hint or explanation seems strange, check it against your textbook, your teacher, or another trusted source.
2. **Follow the rules.** Some schools and teachers limit AI use. Read the rules, and be honest about how you use AI.

**In short:** Try first, ask for hints, practice with questions, and keep the thinking for yourself.

lessons.title: 4.2 Activity: “Study Partner Session” & Stretch Task (15 min)
lessons.summary: Use AI as a study partner on a topic you want to learn, write four study prompts, check whether sources can be trusted (with Option A and text-only Option B), and try the Stretch research brief template.
lessons.content:
### Part C: Activity (15 minutes): “Study Partner Session”

> **Your goal:** Use AI as a study partner on a topic that you really want to learn, and then check whether the sources it gives can be trusted. You can use a chatbot and a web browser, or you can use the text-only version in Step 3.

---

#### Step 1: Choose a topic (3 minutes)
Choose something you are studying or curious about, for example, how solar panels work, how vaccines were developed, how a bill becomes law, or the causes of a historical event. Pick a topic that does not need private information.

| Field | My answer |
| :--- | :--- |
| **My topic** | *(Write your topic here)* |
| **What I already know (one or two sentences)** | *(Write what you already know)* |

---

#### Step 2: Write four study prompts (6 minutes)
Write one prompt for each purpose. Use what you learned in Modules 1 to 3, such as audience, format, and limits.

| # | Purpose | My prompt |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **1** | Explain the topic at my level | *(Write your prompt)* |
| **2** | Quiz me with one question at a time | *(Write your prompt)* |
| **3** | Teach-back: find what I misunderstand | *(Write your prompt)* |
| **4** | Summarize with sources that I can check | *(Write your prompt)* |

---

#### Step 3: Check the sources (4 minutes)

##### Option A: With a chatbot and a browser
Run your fourth prompt. Choose two sources that the AI gave. Search for each one, open it, and complete the table.

| Source the AI gave | Did I find it? (yes or no) | Does it say what the AI claimed? | My decision (use or do not use) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Source 1** | | | |
| **Source 2** | | | |

##### Option B: Text-only version
Read the sample AI answer below. All three sources were **invented for this exercise**, so searching for them will not find real results. The goal is to practice noticing the warning signs.

> **Sample AI answer:**
> Solar panels turn sunlight into electricity using photovoltaic cells. Most panels use silicon. When light hits the silicon, it knocks electrons loose, which creates an electric current. Panels work best in direct sun, but they still produce some power on cloudy days.

| # | Sources listed by the AI |
| :--- | :--- |
| **1** | International Energy Agency, “Introduction to Solar Photovoltaics”, 2019. |
| **2** | “A study by leading scientists shows that solar panels are 100% efficient in bright light.” |
| **3** | Dr. Helena Marwick, “The Silicon Revolution: How Light Became Power”, Greenfield Press, 2017. |

For each source, answer: (a) Does it give enough detail to be searched? (b) What warning signs do you see? (c) What would you do next?

| # | Enough detail to search? | Warning signs | What I would do next |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **1** | | | |
| **2** | | | |
| **3** | | | |

---

#### Step 4: Reflect (2 minutes)
- Which of the four prompts helped you learn the most, and why?
- What would you do differently when a source cannot be found?

---

### Answer Guide and Feedback

#### Sample study prompts (topic: solar panels)
| # | Purpose | Sample prompt |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **1** | Explain | “Explain how solar panels work to a beginner with no science background, in five short sentences, with one everyday comparison.” |
| **2** | Quiz me | “Quiz me on how solar panels work with five questions, one at a time. Wait for my answer, say whether it is right, and explain briefly.” |
| **3** | Teach-back | “I will explain how solar panels work in my own words. Tell me what is missing or wrong, but do not give me the full answer first. My explanation: [text].” |
| **4** | Summarize with sources | “Summarize how solar panels work in five bullet points. For each point, name a real source that I can find, with the organization, title, and year. If you are not sure that a source exists, say so.” |

#### Text-only source review
| # | Sample analysis |
| :--- | :--- |
| **1** | Detailed enough to search: it names an organization, a title, and a year. Warning sign: a detailed look is not proof. Search the organization’s own website for the exact title. If you cannot find it, treat it as unverified. Here it was invented, so you would not find it. |
| **2** | Not enough detail: no author, no title, no date, and no link. The claim of “100% efficient” is also not believable, since no real machine converts all energy perfectly. Next step: do not use it, and look for a real, named source. |
| **3** | Detailed enough to search: author, title, publisher, and year. Warning sign: all of these details can be invented, and they look very convincing. Next step: search for the title and the author, and check a library or bookseller listing. If nothing is found, do not use it. |

#### What good answers show
- The study prompts include the audience, the format, and a clear purpose.
- The learner opens sources (or looks for warning signs) instead of trusting them.
- The learner understands that a detailed-looking source can still be invented.

#### Feedback to show learners
- **Automated check:** All four prompts are written, and the source table has a decision for each source.
- **Feedback:** “Good work. Using AI to practice and to get feedback helps you learn, and checking sources keeps your work honest. Remember: if you cannot find it, do not use it.”

---

### Stretch Task
Build a **research brief template** with four columns: `Question`, `Source`, `Claim`, and `Checked (yes or no)`. Use it on one real question, and record at least three sources.

> **Instructor notes:**
> - This is a practice activity that supports the portfolio’s learning or research entry. It is not rubric-graded.
> - Real chatbots vary in how often they invent sources, so accept honest results.
> - The sources in the text-only version are invented on purpose. Make that clear, so that learners do not think they are real.

Ask the AI to say they are real
quiz_questions.explanation: A source is only a source if you can find and open it.

quiz_questions.question: Why can a source with an author, title, and year still be unreliable?
options: Sources with years are always old
Chatbots can invent sources that look real
quiz_questions.explanation: Detailed-looking sources can be made up, so verify them.

quiz_questions.question: Why is it helpful to paste real text and ask the AI to summarize that text?
options: It removes the need to read anything
The summary is based on a source that you can check, not on the AI’s memory
quiz_questions.explanation: Working from real text keeps the answer tied to something you can compare.

quiz_questions.question: Which question helps you find a one-sided answer?
quiz_questions.explanation: Asking for other viewpoints reveals what the first answer left out.

quiz_questions.question: What does “over-reliance” mean?
options: Depending on AI so much that you stop thinking and learning for yourself
quiz_questions.explanation: Over-reliance can leave you with finished work but little understanding.

quiz_questions.question: Which approach usually helps you learn the most?
options: Asking for the final answer immediately
Trying first, and then asking for a hint or feedback
quiz_questions.explanation: Making your own effort first helps you remember.

quiz_questions.question: What is the idea of the “hint ladder”?
options: Ask for the whole solution first
Climb a real ladder while studying
Ask for a small hint first, and only ask for more help if you are still stuck
Ask the same question five times
quiz_questions.explanation: Starting small keeps your own thinking involved.

quiz_questions.question: True or false: If an AI explains something confidently, you do not need to check it against a trusted source.
quiz_questions.explanation: AI can be wrong with great confidence, so compare important explanations with a trusted source.

quiz_questions.question: How should you use AI for schoolwork that you hand in?
options: Follow your school’s rules, and be honest about how you used it
Say that you did everything alone if you used AI
quiz_questions.explanation: Honesty and following the rules are part of responsible use.

quiz_questions.question: Which is a good prompt for the “compare views” step?
options: “Here are summaries of two articles. List where they agree and where they differ.”
quiz_questions.explanation: A clear comparison prompt helps you see agreement and differences.

quiz_questions.question: Who should write the final conclusion in a research task?
quiz_questions.explanation: AI can give feedback, but the conclusion is your own thinking.

quiz_questions.question: True or false: A source with an author, a title, and a year is always real.
quiz_questions.explanation: All of those details can be invented, so you must still find and open the source.

quiz_questions.question: Which source is easiest to verify?
options: One that names the organization, the exact title, and the year
quiz_questions.explanation: Specific details let you search for the source, but you still need to check that it exists.

quiz_questions.question: The AI says a claim is supported by a study, but you cannot find the study anywhere. What should you do?
options: Use it anyway, because the AI sounded sure
Change the study’s name to something similar
Assume it exists in a private library
Do not use it, and mark it as unverified
quiz_questions.explanation: If you cannot find it, do not use it.

quiz_questions.question: Which prompt asks for missing perspectives?
options: “What viewpoints or evidence are missing from this answer?”
quiz_questions.explanation: This kind of question helps you spot gaps and bias.

lessons.title: 5.1 Lesson & Reading: Checking and Improving Output & “The Iteration Log” (20 min)
lessons.summary: Check AI output with the A-C-F-R test, spot hallucinations, missing context, bias, and outdated info, turn mistakes into better prompts, and keep private information out.
lessons.content:
**COURSE 2 | PART 1: TEXT PROMPTING**
**Module 5: Checking and Improving Output**
*Written lesson and reading (20 minutes)*

| Item | Details |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Module time** | 50 minutes: written lesson (12 min), reading (8 min), activity (15 min), knowledge check (15 min) |
| **Level** | Beginner to Intermediate. Modules 1 to 4 are helpful |
| **Tools** | A web browser is needed for the activity. A chatbot is optional |
| **Format** | Written lesson with tables, a short reading, a fact-checking activity, and a quiz |

---

### Part A: The Lesson (12 minutes)

> **What you will learn:** By the end of this lesson, you will be able to check AI output with a four-part test, spot hallucinations, missing context, and bias, turn each mistake into a better prompt, and avoid sharing information that should stay private.

#### 1. Good-looking is not the same as good
First, let’s face a simple fact. AI output almost always looks good. It is well organized, it uses confident words, and it rarely says “I don’t know.” Nevertheless, the answer can still contain wrong facts, leave out important things, or be unfair. Therefore, a good prompter does not only write good prompts. A good prompter also checks the result and improves the prompt when something goes wrong.

#### 2. The four-check test
To make checking easy, you can use four questions. Together, they spell a simple memory aid: **A-C-F-R**.

| Check | Question | What to look for |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Accurate** | Are the facts correct? | Names, dates, numbers, quotes, links, and advice. Check the ones that matter |
| **Complete** | Is anything important missing? | Missing warnings, steps, costs, or viewpoints |
| **Fair** | Is it balanced and respectful? | Stereotypes, one-sided views, or assumptions about people |
| **Right for the audience** | Does it fit the reader and the purpose? | Tone, level, length, and safety for the people who will use it |

For quick, low-stakes tasks, a fast look may be enough. In contrast, for anything that other people will read or rely on, use all four checks.

#### 3. Four common problems
| Problem | What it looks like | Warning signs |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Hallucination** | A made-up fact, quote, source, or link that sounds real | Very exact details that you cannot find anywhere, and total confidence |
| **Missing context** | A correct-sounding answer that leaves out something that matters | No warnings, no limits, and no “it depends” |
| **Bias** | Stereotypes, or only one viewpoint | Assumptions about gender, age, culture, or places |
| **Outdated information** | Facts that were true earlier but have changed | Laws, prices, news, and “latest” anything |

#### 4. How to check quickly
- **Choose the claims that matter.** You do not have to check every word. Start with names, dates, numbers, quotes, and advice that someone might act on.
- **Cross-check with trusted sources.** For important facts, look for two independent sources, such as official websites, respected news organizations, or encyclopedias.
- **Ask the AI to list its claims.** For example: *“List the factual claims in your answer that I should check.”* This can help, but it never replaces your own checking.
- **Read it as the audience.** Would the reader be confused, offended, or put at risk?
- **Ask a knowledgeable person** for important decisions, such as health, money, law, or safety.

#### 5. Turn every mistake into a better prompt
When you find a problem, do not only fix the result. Instead, ask why the AI made the mistake, and change the prompt. As a result, your next answer is likely to be better, and your templates get stronger.

| Problem you found | Prompt fix to try |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Invented facts** | “Use only the information I give you. If you are not sure, say ‘I don’t know’ instead of guessing.” |
| **Missing context** | Add the situation, the audience, and what must be included, such as “Include safety warnings.” |
| **Too general** | Add examples, limits, and the format you want |
| **Wrong tone or level** | Name the audience and the tone, such as “for 11-year-olds, friendly and simple.” |
| **Biased or one-sided** | “Include different viewpoints, and avoid stereotypes. Describe people neutrally.” |
| **Outdated** | Paste the current information, or check an up-to-date source yourself |

> **Remember:** A better prompt can reduce mistakes, but it cannot remove them. You still need to check.

#### 6. Privacy and safety in your prompts
In addition to checking the output, you must also think about what you put in. Some information should never go into a prompt:
- Passwords, bank details, and ID numbers.
- Private information about other people, such as addresses, phone numbers, or health details.
- Confidential documents from your school or workplace, unless your organization has approved the tool.

Instead, use placeholders such as `[name]` or made-up details. Also, check the privacy settings of your tool, because some tools may store or use what you type.

#### Being honest
Finally, be honest about how you use AI. If you are asked whether AI helped, say so. Following the rules of your school or workplace is part of using AI responsibly.

#### 7. Knowing when to stop
Sometimes, no amount of prompting fixes a problem. If you have tried two or three improved prompts and the answer is still wrong, stop. Then, you can do the task yourself, use a different source, or ask an expert.

#### Key takeaways
- AI output looks good even when it is wrong, so always check what matters.
- Use the A-C-F-R test: accurate, complete, fair, and right for the audience.
- Common problems are hallucinations, missing context, bias, and outdated information.
- Turn each mistake into a prompt fix, and keep private information out of prompts.
- If repeated tries do not work, change your approach.

#### New words in this lesson
| Word | Meaning |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Claim** | A statement that says something is true, such as a fact, a date, or a number |
| **Hallucination** | A confident answer that is false or made up |
| **Bias** | An unfair or unbalanced tendency in output |
| **Cross-check** | Confirming a fact in more than one trusted source |
| **Iteration** | Improving a prompt step by step, based on the results |
| **Placeholder** | A made-up or blank item, such as `[name]`, used instead of real private information |

---

### Part B: Reading (8 minutes): “The Iteration Log”

When you improve a prompt, it is easy to forget what you changed and why. After a few tries, you may not remember which version worked best. That is why many experienced prompters keep a simple **iteration log**.

An iteration log is a small table where you record each version of your prompt, the result, the problem, and the fix. It takes only a minute per version, but it gives you three benefits. First, you can see what really worked. Second, you can turn the best version into a template (Module 3). Third, it becomes evidence of your thinking in the final portfolio.

#### An example log
| Version | Prompt | Result | Problem | Fix for next time |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **1** | “Write a welcome email for my club.” | Long and formal | Wrong tone, too long | Add audience, tone, and a word limit |
| **2** | “Write a 100-word friendly welcome email for new members of a hiking club.” | Better, but invented a meeting time | Made-up detail | Give the real meeting times, and say not to invent details |
| **3** | “…Use only these meeting times: [times]. Do not add anything else.” | Correct and friendly | None | Save as a template |

#### Your own log
| Version | Prompt | Result | Problem | Fix for next time |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **1** | | | | |
| **2** | | | | |
| **3** | | | | |

#### Tips for a useful log
- **Change one thing at a time.** Then you can see which change made the difference.
- **Be specific about the problem.** Write “invented a date,” not “bad.”
- **Keep the good versions.** Save the best prompt as a template, with a “when to use it” line.
- **Keep private data out.** Use placeholders in the log, too.

**In short:** Write down the prompt, the result, the problem, and the fix. It takes a minute and saves much more.

lessons.title: 5.2 Activity: “Fact-Check and Refine” & Stretch Task (15 min)
lessons.summary: Mark and check claims in a Mount Everest fact sheet, apply the A-C-F-R test, write an improved prompt with an iteration log, and try the Stretch test-set task.
lessons.content:
### Part C: Activity (15 minutes): “Fact-Check and Refine”

> **Your goal:** Read an AI answer that contains hidden problems. Check it with the A-C-F-R test, find the mistakes, and rewrite the prompt so that the next answer is better. You need a web browser. A chatbot is optional.

---

#### The situation
A school newsletter editor asked an AI tool to write a short fact sheet about Mount Everest for children aged 10 to 12. The prompt was: *“Write a short fact sheet about Mount Everest.”* Here is the AI’s answer. It was written for this exercise to include mistakes.

> **AI answer:**
> Mount Everest is the highest mountain on Earth above sea level, at about 8,849 meters. It lies on the border between Nepal and India. Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay were the first people to reach the summit, in 1963. Today, hundreds of climbers try the climb each year, and the climbing season is in the autumn, when the weather is warmest. Climbing Everest is easy for beginners with a good guide.

---

#### Step 1: Mark the claims (3 minutes)
Read the answer. Underline every claim that you could check, such as places, dates, numbers, and advice.

#### Step 2: Check the claims (6 minutes)
Use a search engine and trusted sources, such as an encyclopedia or an official mountaineering or government page. For each claim, decide if it is right, wrong, or unsure, and note your source.

| Claim | Right, wrong, or unsure? | Source I used | Correct version |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Height of about 8,849 meters | | | |
| On the border of Nepal and India | | | |
| First climbed by Hillary and Tenzing in 1963 | | | |
| Climbing season is autumn, “when the weather is warmest” | | | |
| “Easy for beginners with a good guide” | | | |

#### Step 3: Apply the A-C-F-R test (2 minutes)
| Check | What I found |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Accurate** | |
| **Complete** (what is missing?) | |
| **Fair** | |
| **Right for the audience** (ages 10 to 12) | |

#### Step 4: Rewrite the prompt (4 minutes)
Write an improved prompt that would lead to a better fact sheet. Use what you found. Think about the audience, safety, and what to do when the AI is unsure. Then, add your changes to an iteration log (Version 1 is the original prompt, and Version 2 is yours).

| Field | My answer |
| :--- | :--- |
| **My improved prompt (Version 2)** | |
| **The problem that I fixed** | |
| **What I will still check myself** | |

If you have a chatbot, run your improved prompt and check the new answer with A-C-F-R. If not, explain in one sentence what you expect to improve.

---

### Answer Guide and Feedback

| Claim | Result |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Height of about 8,849 meters** | **Right.** The officially accepted height is about 8,849 meters, which was confirmed in a 2020 measurement agreed by Nepal and China |
| **On the border of Nepal and India** | **Wrong.** Everest is on the border between Nepal and China (the Tibet Autonomous Region) |
| **First climbed in 1963** | **Wrong.** Hillary and Tenzing Norgay reached the summit in 1953, not 1963 |
| **Autumn is the season, “when the weather is warmest”** | **Misleading.** Most expeditions climb in spring (around April and May), before the summer monsoon. There is a smaller window in autumn. The weather is extremely cold at the summit in any season |
| **“Easy for beginners with a good guide”** | **Wrong and unsafe.** Climbing Everest is extremely dangerous and demanding, even for very experienced climbers. This sentence could give children a false idea |

#### A-C-F-R summary
- **Accurate:** three factual errors (the border, the year, the season) and one dangerous statement.
- **Complete:** there is nothing about the risks, the cold, the thin air, or the cost and preparation.
- **Fair:** there is no obvious bias, but the answer leaves out the people who live and work in the region, such as the Sherpa guides. A fuller answer would mention them.
- **Right for the audience:** the safety claim is not suitable for 10- to 12-year-olds.

#### A sample improved prompt (Version 2)
> “Write a fact sheet about Mount Everest for children aged 10 to 12, in six short bullet points and simple words. Use only facts that you are very confident about, and write ‘I am not sure’ if you are unsure. Include one bullet about how dangerous climbing is, and one about the Sherpa guides who work there. List the facts that I should check before I publish.”

#### What good answers show
- The learner checks each claim with a real source, and finds at least three of the problems.
- The improved prompt names the audience, asks for caution when unsure, and requests safety information.
- The learner knows that they must still check the new answer, because a better prompt does not remove all errors.

#### Feedback to show learners
- **Automated check:** The claim table is filled in, and the improved prompt has at least 25 words.
- **Feedback:** “Good work. Checking claims and then improving the prompt is the core skill of this module. Keep an iteration log, and remember that you are responsible for the final result.”

---

### Stretch Task
Design a small **test set of five different inputs** for one of your prompts, such as five different topics for a summary. Run the prompt on each one, check the results with A-C-F-R, and record where it fails.

> **Instructor notes:**
> - This is a practice activity that supports the portfolio. It is not rubric-graded.
> - The AI answer was written on purpose to include errors. Please verify the facts in the answer guide against current sources before each term.
> - If learners have no internet access, let them use the answer guide after they try the claims themselves, and discuss why checking matters.

quiz_questions.question: Why is it risky to trust AI output only because it looks professional?
options: It can look polished and confident while still containing wrong or missing information
Looks decide whether facts are true
quiz_questions.explanation: Good looks and correctness are two different things.

quiz_questions.question: What do the letters A-C-F-R stand for?
options: Accurate, Complete, Fair, and Right for the audience
quiz_questions.explanation: The four-check test covers facts, gaps, fairness, and fit.

quiz_questions.question: Which of these is a hallucination?
options: A confident quote or source that does not exist
quiz_questions.explanation: A hallucination is a confident answer that is false or made up.

quiz_questions.question: What does “missing context” look like?
options: An answer that is too long
A correct-sounding answer that leaves out something important, such as a warning
quiz_questions.explanation: Missing context can make an answer incomplete or even unsafe.

quiz_questions.question: Which is an example of bias in output?
options: A stereotype about a group of people
quiz_questions.explanation: Bias is an unfair or unbalanced tendency, such as stereotypes.

quiz_questions.question: Why might an AI answer about a recent law be wrong?
options: Its information may be outdated, so you should check an up-to-date source
quiz_questions.explanation: Models can lack recent information.

quiz_questions.question: Which claims should you check first?
options: Nothing, as long as it sounds good
Names, dates, numbers, quotes, and advice that someone may act on
quiz_questions.explanation: Start with the claims that matter most.

quiz_questions.question: How can you cross-check an important fact?
options: Read it again in the same answer
Find it in two independent, trusted sources
quiz_questions.explanation: Independent sources give you more confidence.

quiz_questions.question: True or false: Asking the AI to list claims you should check replaces the need to check them yourself.
quiz_questions.explanation: It can help you plan the checking, but you still have to verify the claims.

quiz_questions.question: Which prompt fix helps reduce invented facts?
options: “Use only the information I give you, and say ‘I don’t know’ if you are not sure.”
quiz_questions.explanation: This kind of instruction discourages guessing, although it cannot remove all errors.

quiz_questions.question: The tone of the answer is too formal for children. What is the best prompt fix?
options: Name the audience and tone, such as “for 11-year-olds, friendly and simple”
quiz_questions.explanation: Naming the audience and tone fixes the fit.

quiz_questions.question: What does an iteration log record?
options: The prompt, the result, the problem, and the fix for each version
quiz_questions.explanation: A log shows what you changed and why.

quiz_questions.question: Why is it a good idea to change one thing at a time when improving a prompt?
options: You can see which change made the difference
quiz_questions.explanation: Single changes make cause and effect visible.

quiz_questions.question: Which information should you never put into a prompt?
options: Passwords, bank details, ID numbers, and private details about other people
quiz_questions.explanation: Private data may be stored or used by the tool.

quiz_questions.question: What can you use instead of real private details in a prompt?
options: Placeholders or made-up details, such as [name]
quiz_questions.explanation: Placeholders let you ask for help without sharing private data.

quiz_questions.question: You tried three improved prompts and the answer is still wrong. What is the best next step?
options: Keep repeating the same prompt forever
Change your approach: do it yourself, use a different source, or ask an expert
quiz_questions.explanation: Sometimes prompting is not the right solution.

quiz_questions.question: True or false: A better prompt can completely remove all errors from AI output.
quiz_questions.explanation: Better prompts reduce problems, but you still need to check the result.

quiz_questions.question: A fact sheet for children says that a dangerous activity is “easy.” Which check does this fail most clearly?
options: Right for the audience, because it could mislead and put children at risk
Title, because it has a name
quiz_questions.explanation: Safety and fit for the audience are part of the check.

quiz_questions.question: When should you be most careful to involve a knowledgeable person?
options: For important decisions about health, money, law, or safety
quiz_questions.explanation: High-stakes decisions need more than AI and a quick check.

quiz_questions.question: If someone asks whether AI helped with your work, what should you do?
options: Say no even if AI helped
Be honest, and follow the rules of your school or workplace
quiz_questions.explanation: Honesty about AI use is part of responsible use.
