lessons.title: 6.1 Lesson & Reading: Prompting for Images & “One Change at a Time” (20 min)
lessons.summary: Write an image prompt with eight useful parts, iterate one change at a time, use style sheets for consistency, know tool limits, and write accessible alt text.
lessons.content:
**COURSE 2 | PART 2: IMAGES, AUDIO, AND VIDEO**
**Module 6: Prompting for Images**
*Written lesson and reading (20 minutes)*

| Item | Details |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Module time** | 50 minutes: written lesson (12 min), reading (8 min), activity (15 min), knowledge check (15 min) |
| **Level** | Beginner to Intermediate. Modules 1 and 2 are helpful |
| **Tools** | An image tool is helpful for the activity but not required. A text-only version is included, with sample results described in words |
| **Format** | Written lesson with tables, a short reading, a prompt-rewriting activity, and a quiz |

> **Access and fairness:** Image tools often have limits, accounts, or costs, and their rules change. You do not have to pay for anything, because every task has a text-only version. Please do not use a real person’s face in your work without their permission.

---

### Part A: The Lesson (12 minutes)

> **What you will learn:** By the end of this lesson, you will be able to write an image prompt with eight useful parts, improve it by changing one thing at a time, know the common limits of image tools, and write alt text so that your images are accessible.

#### 1. How image tools respond to your words
First, let’s connect this lesson to what you already know. In earlier modules, you learned that a text prompt works best when it is clear and complete. The same idea applies to images. An image tool turns your written description into a picture, using patterns that it learned from very many pictures and their descriptions.

However, there is one important difference. When you read text, you can judge the result quickly. With an image, you judge by looking, and small changes in your words can change the picture a lot. In addition, the tool cannot see the picture in your mind. Therefore, every detail that you leave out is chosen for you, and the tool’s choice is often average or generic.

#### 2. The anatomy of an image prompt
To avoid generic results, you can think of an image prompt as having **eight parts**. You do not need all eight every time, but the checklist helps you to remember what to describe.

| Part | Question it answers | Example |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Subject** | What is in the picture? | “a grey tabby cat sleeping” |
| **Setting** | Where and when is it? | “on a windowsill in a sunny kitchen” |
| **Style** | What kind of image is it? | “watercolor illustration” or “realistic photo” |
| **Composition and camera view** | How is it framed? | “close-up from the side” or “view from above” |
| **Lighting** | What is the light like? | “soft morning light” or “warm lamp light at night” |
| **Color and mood** | What colors and feeling? | “warm yellow and cream colors, calm mood” |
| **Format** | What shape or size? | “square image” or “wide image” |
| **What to avoid** | What should not appear? | “no text, no people” |

##### A weak prompt and a strong prompt
| Version | Prompt |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Weak** | “A cat.” |
| **Strong** | “A grey tabby cat sleeping on a windowsill in a sunny kitchen, watercolor illustration style, close-up from the side, soft morning light, warm yellow and cream colors, calm mood, square image, no text.” |

In the strong prompt, the subject, setting, style, composition, lighting, color and mood, format, and exclusions are all named. As a result, the tool has very little to guess.

#### 3. Be specific, not poetic
Next, it helps to describe what can be seen. For instance, an abstract phrase such as *“a feeling of nostalgia”* gives the tool very little to work with. In contrast, *“a faded photo-style picture of an old bicycle leaning on a brick wall, warm sepia colors”* describes things that the tool can draw.
- **Use visible words:** objects, colors, materials, places, and light.
- **Put the most important things first.** Many tools give more weight to the early words.
- **Use a short list of details** instead of a long, flowery sentence.

#### 4. Improve it by changing one thing at a time
After you run a prompt, you will rarely get the perfect picture on the first try. Therefore, you improve it by iteration. The best method is to change **one thing at a time**, such as the lighting or the camera view. Then you can see exactly what each change does. If you change five things at once, you cannot tell which change helped, and you may lose something that you liked.
- **Keep what works.** Write down the version you liked, so that you can return to it.
- **Try variations.** Many tools can make several versions from one prompt, or edit an existing picture, for example *“keep everything, but change the background to a beach.”*
- **Know when to stop.** If a picture is good enough for its purpose, stop.

#### 5. Keeping a set of images consistent
Sometimes, you need several images that belong together, such as pictures for a story or a presentation. Here, consistency is difficult, because each run can look different. A useful approach is to write a **style sheet**, which is a short description that you paste into every prompt.

| Part | Example |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Style sheet** | “Flat vector illustration, pastel colors, thick outlines, soft shadows, no text.” |
| **Character description** | “A round-faced girl with short black hair, a yellow raincoat, and red boots.” |
| **One prompt using both** | “[Style sheet] [Character description] jumping over a puddle in a rainy city street, view from the side.” |

Even so, do not expect a perfect match. Treat consistency as something that you improve, not something that you can guarantee.

#### 6. Common limits of image tools
| Limit | What to do |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Text inside images is often misspelled or distorted** | Ask for “no text”, and add the words later in a design or editing tool |
| **Small details, such as hands, fingers, and tiny objects, can look wrong** | Check carefully, try again, or use a different view, such as a hand holding a cup from a distance |
| **Counting objects may be wrong** | Check the number, and try again if it matters |
| **Real brands, logos, and places may be wrong or may raise legal problems** | Avoid logos and brand names, and use general descriptions |
| **Results vary** | Run again, and record what you really got |

#### 7. Alt text: describing images for everyone
Finally, remember that not everyone can see your image. For example, people who use screen readers hear a description instead. **Alt text** is a short written description of an image. Good alt text says what is shown, includes the important details, and matches the purpose of the image.

| Version | Alt text |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Weak** | “Image of a cat.” |
| **Better** | “A grey tabby cat sleeps on a sunny kitchen windowsill in a soft watercolor illustration, with warm yellow and cream tones.” |

- Keep it to **one or two sentences**.
- **Do not start with “image of” or “picture of”**, because screen readers already say that it is an image.
- Describe what matters for the purpose, not every tiny detail.

#### 8. Responsible use: three quick reminders
- **People:** Do not make or share images of real people without their permission.
- **Labels:** Say that an image is AI-made when you share it.
- **Style and ownership:** Do not try to copy a brand or the style of a living artist. Module 9 covers consent, ownership, and labeling in depth.

#### Key takeaways
- An image prompt has eight parts: subject, setting, style, composition, lighting, color and mood, format, and what to avoid.
- Describe what can be seen, and put the most important things first.
- Improve by changing one thing at a time, and keep what works.
- Use a style sheet for consistency, and expect imperfect results.
- Text, hands, and counting are weak points. Write alt text for every image, and label AI-made images.

#### New words in this lesson
| Word | Meaning |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Subject** | The main thing in the picture |
| **Composition** | How the picture is framed and arranged, including the camera view |
| **Style** | The kind of look, such as a photo, a watercolor, or a flat illustration |
| **Variation** | A different version of the same idea |
| **Style sheet** | A short description of the look that you paste into several prompts to keep images consistent |
| **Alt text** | A short written description of an image for people who cannot see it |

---

### Part B: Reading (8 minutes): “One Change at a Time”

Imagine that you are testing a recipe. If you change the sugar, the oven temperature, and the baking time all at once, and the cake turns out better, you will not know why. If you change only the sugar, you will learn what the sugar does. Improving an image prompt works the same way.

#### An example of four rounds
The table below shows how one prompt can improve over four rounds. The “typical effect” column describes what often happens, but real tools vary.

| Round | What I changed | Typical effect |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **1** | “A lighthouse.” | A generic lighthouse, usually centered, with default style and light |
| **2** | Added the setting and style: “A white lighthouse on a rocky coast, watercolor illustration.” | A more specific scene, with a painted look |
| **3** | Changed only the lighting: “…at sunset, golden light.” | The same scene, with warmer colors and longer shadows |
| **4** | Changed only the camera view: “…seen from below, wide image.” | The same scene, with a more dramatic, taller feeling |

#### Why this works
- **You learn what each word does.** After a few rounds, you build a personal sense of which words change what.
- **You can go back.** If round 4 is worse, you return to round 3 and try something else.
- **You can reuse the result.** The best version becomes a template, and the style part becomes your style sheet.

#### Keep a short log
Use the iteration log from Module 5. For each round, write the prompt, what you saw, what you liked or disliked, and the next change.

| Version | Prompt | Result | Problem | Next change |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **1** | | | | |
| **2** | | | | |
| **3** | | | | |

**In short:** Change one thing, look, decide, and repeat. Keep what works, and stop when the picture is good enough for its purpose.

lessons.title: 6.2 Activity: “Rebuild the Picture” & Stretch Task (15 min)
lessons.summary: Rewrite five weak prompts using the eight-part anatomy, test or compare with the text-only alternative, write alt text, and try the Stretch style-sheet task.
lessons.content:
### Part C: Activity (15 minutes): “Rebuild the Picture”

> **Your goal:** Five weak prompts are paired with five pictures that someone wants. Rewrite each prompt using the eight-part anatomy, and write alt text. If you have an image tool, test two of your prompts. If not, use the text-only version in Step 3.

---

#### Step 1: Read the targets (2 minutes)
Each row shows a weak prompt and the picture that the person really wants.

#### Step 2: Rewrite the prompts (7 minutes)
For each row, write an improved prompt. Use at least five of the eight anatomy parts. Do not include real people or brand names.

| # | Weak prompt | Target picture (what the person wants) | My improved prompt |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **1** | “A library.” | A quiet reading corner by a tall window on a rainy evening, with a green armchair, a steaming cup, warm lamp light, and old books | |
| **2** | “A dog.” | A golden retriever puppy running through orange autumn leaves in a park, looking joyful, in the late afternoon | |
| **3** | “A city.” | A busy night market in a small city, with glowing lanterns and food stalls, seen from above | |
| **4** | “A poster for my club.” | A hiking club poster with mountains at sunrise, bold simple shapes, bright colors, and no text | |
| **5** | “Food.” | A bowl of tomato soup with fresh basil on a rustic wooden table, seen from above, in natural light | |

---

#### Step 3: Test or compare (4 minutes)

##### Option A: With an image tool
Run two of your prompts. For one of them, change **one thing only** (such as the lighting or the camera view) and run it again. Record what changed.

| Prompt I ran | What I changed (one thing) | What the picture did |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| | | |

##### Option B: Text-only version
Two sample results are described in words below. They were written for this exercise, and real tools will give different pictures. Both answer the “dog” row.

| Prompt | Sample result (described in words) |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Weak:** “A dog.” | A dog stands in the middle of the picture in front of a plain grey background. It looks straight at the camera. The light is flat and even, and there are no other objects. |
| **Improved:** “A golden retriever puppy running across a park path covered in orange autumn leaves, caught mid-stride, low camera angle, warm late-afternoon sunlight, shallow depth of field, joyful mood, wide image.” | A golden puppy bounds along a leaf-covered path, with its ears flying. The camera is near the ground, so the leaves in front are slightly blurred. Long golden light falls from the side, and the trees in the background are soft and orange. |

- Which anatomy parts did the improved prompt add?
- What did the weak prompt leave to the tool’s choice?

---

#### Step 4: Write alt text (2 minutes)
Write alt text (one or two sentences) for the improved “dog” picture, or for one of your own results.

| Field | My answer |
| :--- | :--- |
| **My alt text** | |

---

### Answer Guide and Feedback

There is no single correct prompt. Here are sample rewrites.

| # | Sample improved prompt |
| :--- | :--- |
| **1** | “A quiet reading corner by a tall window on a rainy evening, a green armchair, a wooden side table with a steaming cup, a stack of old books, rain on the glass, warm lamp light, cozy mood, soft realistic illustration style, wide image, no people.” |
| **2** | “A golden retriever puppy running through orange autumn leaves in a park, caught mid-stride, low camera angle, warm late-afternoon light, joyful mood, realistic photo style, wide image.” |
| **3** | “A busy night market in a small city, glowing paper lanterns and food stalls, view from above, warm orange and red colors, lively mood, detailed illustration style, wide image, no text, no real brands.” |
| **4** | “A hiking club poster: mountains at sunrise, bold simple flat shapes, bright orange and blue colors, hopeful mood, vertical poster format, no text.” |
| **5** | “A bowl of tomato soup with fresh basil on a rustic wooden table, view from above, soft natural window light, warm red and green colors, realistic photo style, square image.” |

#### Sample alt text for the “dog” picture
> “A golden retriever puppy runs along a park path covered in orange autumn leaves, with long golden light and soft trees behind it.”

#### What good answers show
- Each rewrite uses at least five anatomy parts, and describes things that can be seen.
- The poster prompt asks for “no text”, because text in images is often wrong.
- The alt text describes what is shown in one or two sentences, and it does not start with “image of”.
- No real people or brands are used.

#### Feedback to show learners
- **Automated check:** All five prompts are rewritten with at least 25 words each, and alt text is provided.
- **Feedback:** “Good work. Strong image prompts name what can be seen, and they leave little for the tool to guess. Remember to change one thing at a time, and to write alt text.”

---

### Stretch Task
Write a **style sheet** and a **character description**, and use them in four different prompts for a short story, such as a girl in a yellow raincoat in four different places. Note how consistent the results are.

> **Instructor notes:**
> - This is a practice activity that supports the portfolio’s image entry. It is not rubric-graded.
> - Check the terms and the privacy notice of any image tool you recommend, since they change.
> - Tell learners not to use real people’s faces or brand names, and to label AI-made images when they share them.
> - The sample results in the text-only version are descriptions written for this exercise. Update them if they no longer show a clear difference.

lessons.title: 6.3 Module 6 Knowledge Check (10 Questions from 20-Question Bank)
lessons.summary: 10 questions randomly drawn from the 20-question Module 6 bank (15 minutes).

quiz_questions.question: Why do short, vague image prompts often give generic pictures?
options: The tool chooses every missing detail for you, and its choices are often average
quiz_questions.explanation: Details that you leave out are chosen by the tool.

quiz_questions.question: Which is NOT one of the eight parts of an image prompt in this module?
quiz_questions.explanation: The eight parts are subject, setting, style, composition, lighting, color and mood, format, and what to avoid.

quiz_questions.question: What does “composition and camera view” describe?
options: How the picture is framed, such as a close-up or a view from above
quiz_questions.explanation: Composition says how the scene is framed and arranged.

quiz_questions.question: Which is a better image description?
options: “An old bicycle leaning on a brick wall, warm sepia colors, soft evening light”
quiz_questions.explanation: Visible details are easier for the tool to draw than abstract feelings.

quiz_questions.question: Why should you put the most important words first in an image prompt?
options: Many tools give more weight to the early words
quiz_questions.explanation: Putting key details early helps them to stand out.

quiz_questions.question: What is the best way to improve an image prompt?
options: Change one thing at a time, and look at the result
quiz_questions.explanation: Single changes show what each change does.

quiz_questions.question: You like version 2 of a picture, but version 3 is worse. What should you do?
options: Go back to version 2, and try a different single change
quiz_questions.explanation: Keeping the version that works lets you improve from a good base.

quiz_questions.question: What is a style sheet in this module?
options: A paper form from a school
A short description of the look that you paste into several prompts for consistency
quiz_questions.explanation: A style sheet helps several images to match.

quiz_questions.question: Which is a common weak point of image tools?
options: Text inside images, which is often misspelled
quiz_questions.explanation: It is better to add text later in a design tool.

quiz_questions.question: How can you reduce the risk of misspelled text in an image?
options: Ask for “no text”, and add the words later in an editing tool
Use only capital letters in the prompt
Ask the tool to guess the spelling
quiz_questions.explanation: Adding text yourself gives you control over the spelling.

quiz_questions.question: True or false: Image tools always draw the correct number of objects.
quiz_questions.explanation: Counting can be wrong, so check the picture when the number matters.

quiz_questions.question: What is alt text?
options: A short written description of an image for people who cannot see it
A paper caption on a wall
quiz_questions.explanation: Alt text makes images accessible.

quiz_questions.question: Which alt text is best?
options: “A golden puppy runs along a park path covered in orange autumn leaves.”
quiz_questions.explanation: Good alt text says what is shown, and does not start with “image of.”

quiz_questions.question: How long should alt text usually be?
options: It should not be written at all
quiz_questions.explanation: Alt text should be short and focused on what matters.

quiz_questions.question: You want four pictures of the same character. What helps most?
options: Using a different description each time
A character description and a style sheet pasted into each prompt
quiz_questions.explanation: Repeating the same description helps the pictures to match, but they may still differ.

quiz_questions.question: True or false: A style sheet guarantees that all images will match perfectly.
quiz_questions.explanation: It improves consistency, but results can still differ from image to image.

quiz_questions.question: What should you do before making an image of a real person?
options: Nothing, because it is only AI
Get their permission, or choose a different subject
Post it first and ask later
quiz_questions.explanation: Respect for people and consent matter.

quiz_questions.question: What should you do when you share an AI-made image?
options: Say that it was made with AI
Pretend that you took the photo
Claim it as a real news photo
quiz_questions.explanation: Honest labeling prevents people from being misled.

quiz_questions.question: Why should you avoid brand names and logos in prompts?
options: Brands cannot be drawn in blue
They may come out wrong or may cause legal problems, so use general descriptions
quiz_questions.explanation: General descriptions are safer and often work better.

quiz_questions.question: A tool gives a different picture each time for the same prompt. What does this mean?
options: Results vary, so you should record what you really got
quiz_questions.explanation: Variation is normal, which is why logs and screenshots are useful.

| :--- | :--- |
| **Module time** | 50 minutes: written lesson (12 min), reading (8 min), activity (15 min), knowledge check (15 min) |
| **Level** | Beginner to Intermediate. Modules 1, 2, and 5 are helpful |
| **Tools** | A speech-to-text or text-to-speech tool is helpful for the activity but not required. A text-only version is included |
| **Format** | Written lesson with tables, a short reading, a transcript-and-script activity, and a quiz |

> **Access and fairness:** Audio tools often have limits, accounts, or costs, and their rules change. You never have to pay for anything, because every task has a text-only version. Please do not record or upload other people’s voices without their permission.

---

### Part A: The Lesson (12 minutes)

> **What you will learn:** By the end of this lesson, you will know four ways to use AI with audio, how to prompt for each one, what typically goes wrong, and how to protect the privacy and consent of the people in your recordings.

#### 1. Four ways to use AI with audio
First, let’s look at the big picture. Generative AI can work with sound in several ways. In this module, we focus on four of them.

| Use | What it does | Example |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Speech to text** | Turns spoken words into written text, called a transcript | Transcribing a talk, an interview, or a meeting |
| **Summarizing audio** | Shortens a transcript into the main points and actions | “Five bullet points and who does what” |
| **Text to speech** | Turns a written script into a spoken voice | A voice-over for a video or a spoken announcement |
| **Music and sound** | Creates background music or sound effects from a description | “Calm piano music for a study video” |

#### 2. Speech to text: getting a good transcript
Speech to text is often the first step, because a transcript lets you search, quote, and summarize what was said. It is also good for accessibility, since people who cannot hear the audio can read it.

However, transcripts are not perfect. The tool listens to sounds and guesses the words, so it often makes the same kinds of mistakes.

| Typical problem | Example and what to do |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Names and unusual words** | “Marcus” becomes “Mercus.” Check names against a list, and fix them |
| **Words that sound alike** | “two” becomes “to,” and “gate” becomes “gait.” Read for meaning, and fix |
| **Accents and fast speech** | Accuracy may drop. Review these parts more carefully |
| **Noise and several speakers** | Wind, music, and people talking at once confuse the tool. Record in a quiet place, with one person speaking at a time |
| **Numbers, dates, and email addresses** | These are easy to mishear and very important. Always check them |

##### Tips for better transcripts
- **Record clearly.** Stay close to the microphone, use a quiet room, and speak at a normal pace.
- **Give the tool a head start.** Some tools let you add a list of names or special words. If yours does, use it.
- **Always review.** Read the transcript while you listen, at least to the parts that matter.

##### A prompt for cleaning a transcript
> “Below is a transcript with possible errors. Fix obvious spelling and word mistakes using the facts sheet. Do not change the meaning, and do not add anything. If a word is unclear, write [unclear]. Facts sheet: [paste facts]. Transcript: [paste transcript].”

#### 3. Summarizing audio
Next, to summarize audio, you usually start with the transcript, and then use a text prompt. This links back to what you learned in Module 3. For example:
> “Summarize the transcript below in five bullet points. Then list the action items in a table with the columns Task, Person, and Deadline. Use only what is in the transcript, and write ‘not stated’ if something is missing. Transcript: [paste transcript].”

- **Check against the transcript.** A summary can drop or change points.
- **Remember the chain.** If the transcript has errors, the summary will also have them. Therefore, fix the transcript first.
- **Check who said what.** Speaker labels are often wrong in meetings with several people.

#### 4. Text to speech: from script to voice
Now, let’s turn to text to speech. Here, you write a script, and the tool reads it aloud in a synthetic voice. You can often choose the voice, the pace, and the tone. For a good result, **write for the ear**, because text that reads well on a page may sound awkward when spoken. The next reading explains how.
- **Choose a voice that fits.** A calm, slow voice suits a study guide, and a lively voice suits an event announcement.
- **Add pronunciation notes** for names and unusual words, such as *“Siobhan (shuh-VAWN).”*
- **Listen to the whole thing.** Mistakes in stress and pacing are easy to hear, and hard to see.
- **Label it.** Tell listeners that the voice is AI-generated.

#### 5. Music and sound prompts
You can also describe music or sound effects in words. As with images, a good prompt names the important parts. Six useful parts are shown below.

| Part | Example |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Genre** | “lo-fi,” “acoustic folk,” or “orchestral” |
| **Mood** | “calm and focused” or “bright and hopeful” |
| **Tempo** | “slow,” “medium,” or “fast” |
| **Instruments** | “soft piano and light percussion” |
| **Length and structure** | “30 seconds, with a gentle start and a clear ending” |
| **What to avoid** | “no vocals, no sudden loud sounds” |

For example: *“Calm lo-fi study music, slow tempo, soft piano and light percussion, 30 seconds with a gentle start and a clear ending, no vocals.”* As with images, improve by changing one thing at a time, and record what each change did.
- **Results vary.** Run it again, and record what you really got.
- **Check the rules.** Tools have terms about how you may use the music. Read them before you publish.
- **Avoid copying.** Do not ask for a copy of a particular song, for someone else’s lyrics, or for the voice of a real artist. Module 9 covers ownership and consent.

#### 6. Consent and privacy come first
Finally, sound is personal. A voice can identify a person, and a recording can contain private information. Therefore, think about the people in your audio before you record or upload.
- **Ask permission** before you record someone, and before you upload their voice to a tool. Rules about recording differ between places and organizations, so ask, and follow the rules that apply.
- **Keep sensitive recordings out.** Do not upload private conversations, such as health, legal, or personal talks.
- **Never imitate a real person’s voice without their permission.** Voice imitation can be used to trick people, and it can seriously harm someone’s trust and reputation.
- **Label synthetic voices.** Say when a voice is AI-generated.
- **Delete what you no longer need.** Check how your tool stores recordings.

#### 7. Accessibility benefits
On the positive side, audio tools can make content more accessible. Transcripts and captions help people who are deaf or hard of hearing, people who are learning a language, and anyone who prefers to read. Text to speech helps people who find reading difficult. So, whenever you publish audio, offer a transcript.

#### Key takeaways
- Four audio uses are speech to text, summarizing audio, text to speech, and music or sound prompts.
- Transcripts often contain errors in names, similar-sounding words, numbers, and dates, so always check them.
- Fix the transcript before you summarize it, because errors carry over.
- Write scripts for the ear, add pronunciation notes, and label synthetic voices.
- Ask permission before recording or uploading a voice, never imitate a real person’s voice, and keep private recordings out of tools.

#### New words in this lesson
| Word | Meaning |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Transcript** | A written version of spoken words |
| **Speech to text** | Technology that turns spoken words into written text |
| **Text to speech** | Technology that reads written text aloud in a synthetic voice |
| **Synthetic voice** | A voice made by AI, not recorded from a person |
| **Pronunciation note** | A short guide to how a word should sound, such as “Siobhan (shuh-VAWN)” |
| **Tempo** | The speed of music |
| **Consent** | Permission from a person before you record, use, or copy their voice or image |

---

### Part B: Reading (8 minutes): “Write for the Ear”

Written text and spoken text are different. When you read a page, your eyes can go back, skim ahead, and pause on a hard sentence. When you listen, you hear each word once, in order. Therefore, a script that looks perfect on paper can sound confusing when it is read aloud.

#### Six rules for scripts
1. **Use short sentences.** Aim for about 15 words, with one idea in each.
2. **Write numbers and dates the way you say them.** Write “ten in the morning” instead of “10:00,” and “the eighteenth of May” instead of “18/5.”
3. **Avoid symbols and abbreviations.** Write “percent” instead of “%,” and “for example” instead of “e.g.”
4. **Repeat the key point.** Listeners cannot scroll back, so say the date, place, or action twice.
5. **Add pronunciation notes** for names and unusual words.
6. **Read it aloud before you use it.** If you stumble, the tool will probably stumble too.

#### Before and after
| Version | Text |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Written for the eye** | “The Q3 results (see p. 4) show a 12% increase in sales vs. last year; attendance was 1,250 on 18/5.” |
| **Written for the ear** | “Our sales grew by twelve percent compared with last year. That is good news. On the eighteenth of May, one thousand two hundred and fifty people came.” |

#### Marking pauses and emphasis
Many tools respond to punctuation. A comma gives a short pause, and a full stop gives a longer one. Some tools also accept notes such as `[pause]`. Check what your tool supports, and listen to the result.

#### An example with pronunciation notes
> “Welcome, everyone. Our guest today is Siobhan (shuh-VAWN) Ó Briain (oh BREE-un). She will talk about the new library. Please welcome Siobhan.”

Notice that the name is repeated, so that listeners remember it, and that the notes show how to say it.

**In short:** Short sentences, spoken numbers, repeated key points, and pronunciation notes. Always listen before you publish.

lessons.title: 7.2 Activity: “Script and Transcript Check” & Stretch Task (15 min)
lessons.summary: Find and fix five errors in an AI transcript using a facts sheet, write a clean-and-summarize prompt, draft a voice script for the ear, and try the Stretch 6-part music prompt task.
lessons.content:
### Part C: Activity (15 minutes): “Script and Transcript Check”

> **Your goal:** Fix errors in an AI transcript, write a prompt that cleans and summarizes it, and prepare a short voice script that is written for the ear. If you have a speech tool, you can use it for Step 3. If not, read your script aloud yourself.

---

#### Step 1: Find and fix the errors (4 minutes)
An AI tool transcribed a 40-second announcement, recorded outdoors on a windy day. The transcript has **five errors**. Compare it with the organizer’s facts sheet.

| | |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Facts sheet (correct information)** | Speaker: Marcus, from the Maple Park Neighbors group. Event: community cleanup day on Saturday, 18 May, at 10 a.m. Meeting place: the north gate by the playground. Bring gloves, and a wheelbarrow if you have one. Two volunteers are needed for the snack table. To help, email marcus at maplepark dot example by Wednesday. |
| **AI transcript (with errors)** | Hi everyone, this is Mercus from the Maple Park Neighbors group. Our next cleanup day is Saturday the eighteenth of May at tent a.m. We meet at the north gait by the playground. Please bring gloves, and if you have one, a wheelbarrow. We also need to volunteers to help with the snack table. If you can help, email marcus at maple park group dot org by Wednesday. Thanks, and see you there! |

| # | Wrong text in the transcript | Correct text | Why the tool may have made this mistake |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **1** | | | |
| **2** | | | |
| **3** | | | |
| **4** | | | |
| **5** | | | |

---

#### Step 2: Write a clean-and-summarize prompt (4 minutes)
Write one prompt that asks an AI tool to (a) fix the transcript using the facts sheet without changing the meaning, and (b) summarize it in three bullet points with the action items in a table. Use what you learned in this module and in Modules 1 to 3.

| Field | My answer |
| :--- | :--- |
| **My prompt** | |

---

#### Step 3: Write a voice script (5 minutes)
Write a short script (about 40 words) for a different announcement, such as a school event or a club meeting. Use made-up details. Follow the rules for writing for the ear, and add a pronunciation note for at least one name or unusual word.

| Field | My answer |
| :--- | :--- |
| **My announcement script** | |
| **My pronunciation note(s)** | |
| **Voice choice (pace and tone) and why** | |

**Test it:**
- **Option A:** Run your script through a text-to-speech tool, listen, and note one thing to fix.
- **Option B (text-only):** Read it aloud yourself, and mark any place where you stumbled or ran out of breath.

---

#### Step 4: Consent and reflection (2 minutes)
- Who is speaking in the recording? Did they agree to be recorded and transcribed?
- How will you label a voice that is AI-generated?
- Which correction in Step 1 would have been hardest to notice without the facts sheet?

---

### Answer Guide and Feedback

| # | Wrong text | Correct text | Likely reason |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **1** | Mercus | Marcus | Names are often mis-spelled when they are unusual or spoken in wind |
| **2** | tent a.m. | ten a.m. | A sound-alike word, and numbers are easy to mishear |
| **3** | gait | gate | Words that sound alike, so read for meaning |
| **4** | need to volunteers | need two volunteers | “to” and “two” sound the same, and the number changes the meaning |
| **5** | maple park group dot org | maplepark dot example | Email addresses are often mis-heard, so always check them against the source |

#### A sample clean-and-summarize prompt
> “Below is a transcript of a short announcement that may contain errors. Fix obvious spelling and word mistakes using the facts sheet, but do not change the meaning or add anything. If a word is unclear, write [unclear]. Then summarize the announcement in three bullet points, and list the action items in a table with the columns Task, Person, and Deadline. Write ‘not stated’ if something is missing. Facts sheet: [paste facts]. Transcript: [paste transcript].”

#### A sample script written for the ear
> “Hello, neighbors. Our book club meets on Thursday, at seven in the evening. We meet at the library, near the front desk. This month, we read a book by Siobhan (shuh-VAWN) Keane. Please bring your copy. Again, Thursday at seven. See you there!”

#### What good answers show
- The learner finds all five errors and compares them with a facts sheet instead of guessing.
- The prompt tells the AI to keep the meaning, not add anything, use the facts sheet, and mark unclear words.
- The script uses short sentences, spoken numbers and times, a repeated key point, and a pronunciation note.
- The learner thinks about consent and labeling.

#### Feedback to show learners
- **Automated check:** Five rows are filled in, the prompt has at least 30 words, and the script has at least one pronunciation note.
- **Feedback:** “Good work. Audio tools are powerful, but they make predictable mistakes, especially with names, numbers, and email addresses. Check them, write for the ear, and always think about consent.”

---

### Stretch Task
Write a **music prompt** with all six parts (genre, mood, tempo, instruments, length and structure, and what to avoid). Run it, or imagine the result. Then change one part, such as the tempo, and describe how the result changes.

> **Instructor notes:**
> - This is a practice activity that supports the portfolio’s audio entry. It is not rubric-graded.
> - The transcript and the facts sheet were written for this exercise. The event and the people are made up.
> - If you recommend tools, check their terms, privacy notices, and recording rules first. Remind learners to get permission before they record anyone.
> - Provide transcripts for any audio samples that you use.

“to” was written instead of “two,” because the words sound alike

Ask for their permission, and follow the rules that apply
Post it first and ask later

lessons.title: 8.1 Lesson & Reading: Video and Multimodal Prompting & “Think in Shots” (20 min)
lessons.summary: Plan short videos as storyboards of simple shots with an 8-part video prompt, use the two-step method for multimodal inputs (charts/images), protect privacy, and add captions.
lessons.content:
**COURSE 2 | PART 2: IMAGES, AUDIO, AND VIDEO**
**Module 8: Video and Multimodal Prompting**
*Written lesson and reading (20 minutes)*

| Item | Details |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Module time** | 50 minutes: written lesson (12 min), reading (8 min), activity (15 min), knowledge check (15 min) |
| **Level** | Intermediate. Modules 1, 2, and 6 are helpful |
| **Tools** | A video tool and a chatbot that accepts images are helpful but not required. A text-only version is included, with a sample chart |
| **Format** | Written lesson with tables, a short reading, a storyboard-and-chart activity, and a quiz |

> **Access and fairness:** Video tools are often limited, slow, or costly, and their rules change. You never have to pay for anything, because every task has a text-only version. Please do not use real people’s faces or voices, and do not upload private pictures or documents.

---

### Part A: The Lesson (12 minutes)

> **What you will learn:** By the end of this lesson, you will be able to plan and prompt a short video as a series of shots, and to use images, screenshots, charts, and documents as inputs for AI, while checking for misreads and protecting private information.

#### 1. Two big ideas in one module
This module covers two related skills. First, you will learn to prompt AI to create short videos. Second, you will learn to give AI different kinds of input, such as photos, screenshots, charts, and documents, and to ask questions about them. When a tool can work with more than one kind of information, such as text, images, and video, we call it **multimodal**.

#### 2. The parts of a video prompt
A video prompt is similar to an image prompt, but with two extra ingredients: **action** and **camera movement**, because a video changes over time. A good video prompt has the parts below.

| Part | Question it answers | Example |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Scene** | Where and when does it happen? | “a small kitchen at sunrise” |
| **Subject** | Who or what is the focus? | “a ceramic kettle” |
| **Action** | What happens? | “steam rises, and the kettle begins to whistle” |
| **Shot type** | How close is the view? | “close-up” or “wide shot” |
| **Camera movement** | How does the camera move? | “slowly moves in” or “stays still” |
| **Lighting** | What is the light like? | “warm morning light from a window” |
| **Style** | What does it look like? | “realistic, calm, slightly soft focus” |
| **Length and format** | How long and what shape? | “five seconds, wide format” |

For example: *“Close-up of a ceramic kettle on a kitchen stove at sunrise. Steam rises, and the kettle begins to whistle. The camera slowly moves in. Warm morning light from a window, realistic and calm, five seconds, wide format.”*

#### 3. Plan in shots
Next, it helps to remember how film makers work. A short video is not one long scene. It is a series of short **shots**, joined together. Many AI video tools also make short clips, often of only a few seconds. Therefore, the best approach is to plan your video as a **storyboard**: a list of shots, each with one idea.
- **One subject, one action, one camera move per shot.** Simple shots work best.
- **Reuse your style sheet (Module 6)** in every shot prompt, so that the look stays similar.
- **Describe the setting the same way each time**, such as *“the same small kitchen at sunrise.”*
- **Join the shots later in a video editor**, and add text, sound, and music yourself.

#### 4. Common limits of AI video
| Limit | What to do |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Characters and objects change from one clip to the next** | Use short, simple shots, repeat the same description, and accept small differences |
| **Odd motion, such as strange hands, melting objects, or impossible physics** | Watch the clip several times, even frame by frame, and discard clips with problems |
| **Text and signs are often wrong** | Ask for “no text,” and add text later in an editor |
| **Short length** | Plan for several short clips, not one long one |
| **Sound may not match** | Add your own music or voice-over, and label synthetic voices |
| **Results vary and take time** | Test the first shot, before you spend time on all of them |

Because AI video can look very real, honesty matters even more. Label AI-made video, and do not make realistic videos of real people. Module 9 explains why in more depth.

#### 5. Giving AI more than text: multimodal inputs
Now, let’s look at the other side. Many AI tools let you upload a photo, a screenshot, a chart, or a document, and then ask about it. This is very useful. For example, you can ask:
- “Describe this photo in two sentences that I can use as alt text.”
- “This is a screenshot of an error message. Explain in simple words what it means, and what I should try first.”
- “Here is a chart. List the value for each day in a table, then tell me the highest and the lowest.”
- “Here is a photo of my handwritten notes. Type out the text, and mark any words that you cannot read.”
- “Summarize the attached document in five bullet points, and list the numbers that I should double-check.”

#### 6. A two-step method for reading charts and images
However, multimodal tools can **misread**. They may get a number wrong, miss small text, mix up labels, or confidently describe something that is not there. To protect yourself, use a two-step method.

| Step | What to ask |
| :--- | :--- |
| **1. Describe first** | “First, list exactly what you see: the title, the axes, and each value. Say ‘unclear’ if you cannot read something.” |
| **2. Then analyze** | “Now, using only your list, tell me which day is highest and the total.” |

After that, you compare the AI’s list with the original. Check the numbers, the labels, and the units. If you cannot verify a number, do not use it.

#### 7. Privacy: what you upload matters
In addition, pictures and documents often contain more information than you notice. A photo can show faces, a house number, or a car number plate. A screenshot can show names, emails, or passwords. A document can contain confidential details. Therefore:
- **Do not upload** photos of other people without their permission, ID cards, bank documents, or confidential work files.
- **Crop or blur private parts first**, or use a made-up example.
- **Remember hidden information.** Photos can contain location data. Check your tool and device settings.
- **Check the tool’s privacy notice**, because some tools may store or use what you upload.

#### 8. Accessibility with video and images
Finally, remember accessibility. Add **captions** to videos, so that people who cannot hear them can follow. Provide a short description of what happens in the video, for people who cannot see it. Also, write alt text for images that you upload or share.

#### Key takeaways
- A video prompt names the scene, subject, action, shot type, camera movement, lighting, style, and length.
- Plan in shots: one subject, one action, and one camera move per shot. Reuse your style sheet.
- Typical limits are changing characters, odd motion, wrong text, and short clips. Review carefully, and label AI video.
- For charts and images, describe first, then analyze, and always compare the AI’s reading with the original.
- Protect privacy: do not upload faces, IDs, or confidential documents. Add captions and descriptions.

#### New words in this lesson
| Word | Meaning |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Shot** | One continuous piece of video from a single camera view |
| **Storyboard** | A plan of a video as a list of shots, with what we see in each |
| **Camera movement** | How the camera moves in a shot, such as still, panning, or moving in |
| **Multimodal** | Able to work with more than one kind of information, such as text, images, and video |
| **Caption** | Text on a video that shows the words and important sounds |
| **Misread** | When the AI gets a number, a label, or a detail wrong while reading an image or a document |

---

### Part B: Reading (8 minutes): “Think in Shots”

Before you open a video tool, take a pencil and write a **storyboard**. It takes only a few minutes, and it saves a lot of time later. Without a plan, people often try to describe a whole story in one prompt, and the result is a confusing clip.

#### An example storyboard
Here is a four-shot storyboard for a 20-second video called “Morning tea.” Each shot lasts about five seconds.

| Shot | What we see | Camera and shot type | Light and style |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **1** | A small kitchen at sunrise | Wide shot, camera stays still | Warm window light, realistic and calm |
| **2** | A ceramic kettle on the stove, steam rising | Close-up, camera slowly moves in | Warm window light, soft focus |
| **3** | Hot water poured into a cup | Medium shot, camera stays still | Warm window light, realistic |
| **4** | Steam rising from the full cup on a wooden table | Close-up, camera stays still | Warm light, soft background |

#### From storyboard to prompts
Next, turn each row into one prompt. Start every prompt with the same style words, such as *“realistic, calm, warm morning window light, the same small kitchen.”* In this way, the shots look like they belong together.

> **Shot 2 prompt:** “Close-up of a ceramic kettle on a stove in a small kitchen at sunrise. Steam rises and the kettle begins to whistle. The camera slowly moves in. Realistic, calm, warm morning window light, soft focus. Five seconds, wide format, no text.”

#### Tips for good storyboards
- **One idea per shot.** If a shot needs two actions, make it two shots.
- **Vary the shot types.** Mix wide, medium, and close-up views, so that the video feels alive.
- **Test one shot first.** If the style is wrong, fix it before you make the others.
- **Plan the sound separately.** Add music, voice-over, and captions in an editor.
- **Keep a log.** Write the prompt, the result, and the next change for each shot, as in Module 5.

**In short:** Think in shots. Plan first, keep each shot simple, reuse your style, and test one shot before you make them all.

lessons.title: 8.2 Activity: “Storyboard in Prompts” & Stretch Task (15 min)
lessons.summary: Storyboard a 20-second video in four shots with a shared style sheet, check an AI reading of a library visitors chart, and try the Stretch character-and-setting sheet task.
lessons.content:
### Part C: Activity (15 minutes): “Storyboard in Prompts”

> **Your goal:** Plan a 20-second video as four shots, write a prompt for each shot, and then practice reading a chart with the two-step method. You can use a video tool and a chatbot that accepts images, or you can use the text-only version.

---

#### Step 1: Storyboard a 20-second video (7 minutes)
Choose a simple idea that needs no real people, for example a community cleanup, a cup of tea, a plant growing, or a rainy street. Plan four shots of about five seconds each. First, write your shared style sheet.

| Field | My answer |
| :--- | :--- |
| **My video idea** | |
| **Shared style sheet (style, light, setting words to repeat in every shot)** | |

| Shot | What we see (one idea) | Camera and shot type | My prompt for this shot (include the style sheet) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **1** | | | |
| **2** | | | |
| **3** | | | |
| **4** | | | |

- **Option A:** If you have a video tool, run the prompt for Shot 1 only, and watch it more than once. Note anything odd.
- **Option B (text-only):** Reread your Shot 1 prompt, and list three things that could go wrong in the clip, such as a changing object, odd motion, or text.

---

#### Step 2: Read the chart (5 minutes)
The chart below shows the number of visitors to a small library during one week (made-up data). An AI tool read the chart. Its reading is shown below the chart. Compare the reading with the chart, and find the errors.

**Library Visitors (One Week — Chart Data):**
| Day | Mon | Tue | Wed | Thu | Fri | Sat | Sun |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| **Visitors** | 120 | 95 | 140 | 110 | 160 | 210 | 60 |

*Accessibility: A text version of the chart is stored in the image’s alt text, and the course team can give it to you in another format on request.*

> **AI’s reading of the chart:**
> Saturday had the most visitors, at about 210. Wednesday was the busiest weekday, with about 140 visitors. Tuesday had more visitors than Monday. Sunday had the fewest visitors, at about 90. In total, about 895 people visited during the week.

| Claim in the AI’s reading | Right or wrong? | What the chart really shows |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Saturday had the most visitors, at about 210 | | |
| Wednesday was the busiest weekday, with about 140 | | |
| Tuesday had more visitors than Monday | | |
| Sunday had the fewest visitors, at about 90 | | |
| In total, about 895 people visited | | |

- **Optional with a tool:** Upload the chart to a chatbot that accepts images, and use the two-step method: *“First list every bar’s label and value. Then tell me the highest weekday and the total.”* Compare its list with the chart.

---

#### Step 3: Reflect (3 minutes)
- Which of your video shots was simplest, and which was hardest to describe?
- Why is it helpful to ask the AI to describe the chart first, and then analyze?
- How will you label an AI-made video? What would you check before uploading a photo or a document?

---

### Answer Guide and Feedback

#### Chart check
| Claim | Result | What the chart really shows |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Saturday had the most visitors, at about 210** | **Right** | Saturday is the tallest bar, at 210 |
| **Wednesday was the busiest weekday, with about 140** | **Wrong** | Friday was the busiest weekday, with 160. Wednesday had 140 |
| **Tuesday had more visitors than Monday** | **Wrong** | Monday had 120, and Tuesday had 95 |
| **Sunday had the fewest visitors, at about 90** | **Wrong** | Sunday had the fewest, but the value is 60, not 90 |
| **In total, about 895 people visited** | **Right** | 120 + 95 + 140 + 110 + 160 + 210 + 60 = 895 |

Notice that three of the five claims were wrong, even though the reading sounded confident, and one error (Sunday) was a number. This is why the two-step method and your own comparison matter.

#### A sample storyboard (idea: a rainy street)
**Style sheet:** *“realistic, calm, grey-blue evening light, the same quiet city street in light rain, no text, no people.”*

| Shot | What we see | Camera and shot type | Sample prompt |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **1** | A quiet street in light rain | Wide shot, camera still | “Wide shot of a quiet city street in light rain at dusk. Camera stays still. Realistic, calm, grey-blue evening light, no text, no people. Five seconds, wide format.” |
| **2** | Rain drops on a shop window | Close-up, camera still | “Close-up of rain drops running down a shop window on a quiet city street at dusk. Camera stays still. Realistic, calm, grey-blue evening light, no text, no people. Five seconds, wide format.” |
| **3** | A bicycle parked under a lamp | Medium shot, camera slowly moves in | “Medium shot of a bicycle under a street lamp on a quiet rainy street at dusk. Camera slowly moves in. Realistic, calm, grey-blue evening light, no text, no people. Five seconds, wide format.” |
| **4** | A puddle with ripples | Close-up, camera still | “Close-up of a puddle with rain ripples on a quiet city street at dusk. Camera stays still. Realistic, calm, grey-blue evening light, no text, no people. Five seconds, wide format.” |

#### What good answers show
- The storyboard has four simple shots, each with one idea, one action, and one camera move.
- The same style words are used in every shot prompt.
- The learner found at least three of the chart errors, by comparing, and understands that a confident reading can still be wrong.
- The learner thinks about labeling and privacy.

#### Feedback to show learners
- **Automated check:** Four shots are filled in, each prompt has at least 25 words, and the chart table is complete.
- **Feedback:** “Good work. Plan in shots, repeat your style, and compare the AI’s reading of an image with the original. Remember to label AI video and to keep private material out.”

---

### Stretch Task
Write a **character and setting sheet** (a few sentences that describe a made-up character and place), and paste it into all four shot prompts. Note how consistent the shots look, or how consistent you expect them to be.

> **Instructor notes:**
> - This is a practice activity that supports the portfolio’s audio or video entry and the workflow entry. It is not rubric-graded.
> - The chart data are made up. The chart image has alt text and a text version. Check the answer guide, if you change the data.
> - Video tools vary a lot. Accept honest results, including failed clips, and ask learners to describe what went wrong.
> - Remind learners not to use real people, and not to upload private images or documents.

lessons.title: 8.3 Module 8 Knowledge Check (10 Questions from 20-Question Bank)
lessons.summary: 10 questions randomly drawn from the 20-question Module 8 bank (15 minutes).

quiz_questions.question: What does “multimodal” mean?
options: Able to run on many computers at once
Able to work with more than one kind of information, such as text, images, and video
quiz_questions.explanation: Multimodal tools can use more than one type of input.

quiz_questions.question: Which two ingredients make a video prompt different from an image prompt?
quiz_questions.explanation: Videos change over time, so you describe what happens and how the camera moves.

quiz_questions.question: What is a shot?
options: One continuous piece of video from a single camera view
quiz_questions.explanation: A video is a series of shots.

quiz_questions.question: What is a storyboard?
options: A plan of a video as a list of shots, with what we see in each
quiz_questions.explanation: A storyboard helps you plan before you use a tool.

quiz_questions.question: Why is it best to plan a short video as several simple shots?
options: AI video tools often make short clips, and simple shots work better
Tools can only make one-second videos
quiz_questions.explanation: Simple, short shots are easier to control and to join together.

quiz_questions.question: Which is a good rule for a single shot?
options: One subject, one action, one camera move
quiz_questions.explanation: Simple shots are more reliable.

quiz_questions.question: How can you help several shots look like they belong together?
options: Use a different tool for each word
Repeat the same style words and setting description in every shot prompt
quiz_questions.explanation: A shared style sheet improves consistency.

quiz_questions.question: Which is a typical limit of AI video?
options: It cannot show the color blue
It can only make videos with no light
Characters and objects can change between clips, and motion can look odd
quiz_questions.explanation: Review clips carefully and discard those with problems.

quiz_questions.question: How should you handle text that you want in a video?
options: Trust the tool to spell everything
Ask for “no text” in the prompt, and add the text later in an editor
Write the text in very small letters
quiz_questions.explanation: Text in generated video is often wrong, so add it yourself.

quiz_questions.question: What should you do with an AI-made video that looks very realistic?
options: Label it as AI-made, and do not use real people’s likenesses
Say that it is a real recording
quiz_questions.explanation: Honest labeling prevents people from being misled.

quiz_questions.question: What is the two-step method for reading a chart with AI?
options: Ask for the final answer only
First ask the AI to describe what it sees, and then ask it to analyze using only that description
quiz_questions.explanation: Describing first makes misreads easier to spot.

quiz_questions.question: The AI says a chart value is 90, but the bar shows 60. What should you do?
options: Trust the AI because it sounds confident
Trust the chart, not the AI, and correct the reading
quiz_questions.explanation: Always compare the AI’s reading with the original.

quiz_questions.question: Which is a good multimodal prompt?
options: “Here is a screenshot of an error message. Explain in simple words what it means and what to try first.”
quiz_questions.explanation: A clear request tells the AI what to do with the image.

quiz_questions.question: Which should you NOT upload to an AI tool?
options: A photo of your friend’s ID card
A screenshot with private details removed
quiz_questions.explanation: IDs and other private documents should stay out of tools.

quiz_questions.question: What should you do before uploading a screenshot that shows names and emails?
options: Crop or blur the private parts, or use a made-up example
quiz_questions.explanation: Remove private details before you upload.

quiz_questions.question: True or false: A photo can contain hidden information, such as location data.
quiz_questions.explanation: Check your device and tool settings, and remove such information when needed.

quiz_questions.question: What do captions on a video help with?
options: They help people who cannot hear the video to follow it
quiz_questions.explanation: Captions improve accessibility.

quiz_questions.question: Why write a short description of a video or an image?
options: It helps people who cannot see it
It is needed only by the tool
quiz_questions.explanation: Descriptions and alt text help people who use screen readers.

quiz_questions.question: The AI reads three of five chart numbers wrongly, but sounds confident. What does this show?
options: A confident reading can still be wrong, so you must check
quiz_questions.explanation: Check numbers, labels, and units against the original.

quiz_questions.question: True or false: You should test one shot before you make all of the shots in a storyboard.
quiz_questions.explanation: A test shot shows whether the style works, before you spend time on the rest.

sections.title: Checkpoint 2 — Guided Lab 2: Multimedia Prompt Workshop (60 min)

lessons.title: Lab 2 Parts A & B: Image Iteration & Audio Workshop (35 min)
lessons.summary: Iterate an image prompt across 3 one-change-at-a-time rounds + alt text (20 min), and complete an audio transcript/summary or voice script task (15 min). Analysis-only path included.
lessons.content:
> **Guided Lab 2: Multimedia Prompt Workshop (60 minutes total)** — This is your **Part 2 Checkpoint**. Every step includes an **Analysis-Only Path** so no learner is blocked by tool limits or cost. **Do not use real people’s faces or voices.**

---

### Part A: Images — Three Rounds, One Change at a Time (20 minutes)
1. Write a full **8-part image prompt** (Subject, Setting, Style, Composition, Lighting, Color/Mood, Format, Exclusions).
2. Run Round 1 (or use the Sample Output below), then change **one element at a time** across Rounds 2 and 3 (for example: Round 2 changes lighting; Round 3 changes camera angle).
3. Record what each single change did, and write **clear alt text** for your best result.

*(Analysis-Only Sample: Round 1 “ceramic mug on wooden table, daylight” → cluttered background; Round 2 adds “clean blurred café window background” → subject pops; Round 3 changes to “45-degree overhead shot, warm morning light” → balanced composition. Alt text: “Close-up 45-degree photo of a ceramic coffee mug on a wooden café table in warm morning light.”)*

---

### Part B: Audio — Transcript Check or Voice Script (15 minutes)
Choose **one**:
- **Option 1 (Transcript & Summary):** Review an audio transcript (your own non-private sample or Module 7’s sample), list the transcription errors you found, and write a summary prompt.
- **Option 2 (Voice Script):** Write a 60–90 word **ear-ready voice script** with short sentences, spelled-out numbers, and `[pronunciation notes]`. *(Bonus: draft a 6-parameter music bed prompt.)*

lessons.title: Lab 2 Parts C & D: Video/Multimodal & Responsible-Use Debrief (25 min)
lessons.summary: Build a 4-shot video storyboard or multimodal chart check (15 min), then apply Module 9’s five responsible-use questions and complete the Part 2 Self-Check (10 min).
lessons.content:
### Part C: Video or Multimodal Task (15 minutes)
Choose **one** (or both if time allows):
- **Video Storyboard:** Write a **4-shot storyboard in prompts** (4 × 5s clips) for a short explainer, reusing a consistent character/setting note across all 4 shots.
- **Multimodal Check:** Upload a non-private chart or UI screenshot (or use Module 8’s sample chart), ask the AI to extract the data, and log every misread or verified value against the original.

---

### Part D: Responsible-Use Check & Part 2 Self-Check Debrief (10 minutes)
Apply these **five questions** to your Lab 2 outputs in your **Personal Study Notes**:
1. **Who is shown or heard?** *(Confirm no real person’s face or voice was used without consent.)*
2. **Did they agree?**
3. **Who owns or may use the result?** *(Check tool terms.)*
4. **Is it labeled?** *(Write the AI disclosure label you would attach.)*
5. **Could it mislead or harm?**
6. **Part 2 Self-Check:** Confirm you have completed Modules 6–8 and saved alt text / transcripts for accessibility before moving to **Part 3 (Responsible & Advanced Use)**.

sections.title: Part 3 — Module 9: Responsible Use Across Media (50 min)

lessons.title: 9.1 Lesson & Reading: Responsible AI Media & “Label It, Ask First” (20 min)
lessons.summary: Master the 5 responsible-media questions: consent & likeness, ownership & living artists, deepfakes & provenance labeling, bias/stereotypes, safety/privacy, and school/work rules.
lessons.content:
> **What you will learn:** Use AI-generated text, images, audio, and video honestly, safely, and with respect for others. *(12 min lesson + 8 min reading)*

---

### Part A: The Lesson (12 minutes)

#### 1. Five questions before using AI media
| Question | Why it matters | Practical rule |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **1. Who is shown or heard?** | Likeness, face, and voice belong to the person | Never generate or edit a real person’s face or voice without permission |
| **2. Did they agree?** | Consent must be clear and informed | Ask first—especially for classmates, colleagues, or family |
| **3. Who owns or may use the result?** | Laws and tool terms vary by country and plan | Read the tool’s commercial/usage terms; avoid copying living artists’ signature styles |
| **4. Is it labeled?** | Viewers deserve to know what is AI-made | Add clear labels/captions and preserve provenance metadata where supported |
| **5. Could it mislead or harm?** | Deepfakes, stereotypes, and scams cause real harm | Never publish realistic fake news, impersonations, or biased tropes |

#### 2. Bias, Privacy, Provenance & Rules
- **Bias & stereotypes:** Image and voice tools can over-represent stereotypes (e.g., showing only one gender/ethnicity for certain jobs). Check and correct your prompts.
- **Privacy of uploads:** Photos and voice clips you upload may be retained per tool settings—keep IDs and private media out.
- **Provenance labels:** Many tools embed invisible metadata or visible watermarks; keep them intact and follow school/workplace AI policies.

---

### Part B: Reading (8 minutes) — “Label It, Ask First”
When sharing AI media, two habits prevent 90% of problems:
1. **Ask first** whenever a real person’s face, voice, private work, or a team’s rules are involved.
2. **Label it** plainly (*“Image created with AI”*, *“Drafted with AI and verified by the author”*). Honest labeling builds trust.

lessons.title: 9.2 Activity: Case Clinic & Stretch Media Policy (15 min)
lessons.summary: Judge 5 real-world AI media cases (proceed, ask permission, or do not proceed) and write disclosure labels, plus a Stretch 1-page team AI media policy.
lessons.content:
> **Your goal:** Judge the five cases below. For each, decide **Proceed**, **Ask permission**, or **Do not proceed**, explain why, and write a disclosure label if needed. *(15 minutes)*

---

### Five Cases
1. **Voice imitation:** Cloning a manager’s voice without telling them to record a surprise birthday video for the office.
2. **Realistic fake photo:** Posting an AI photo of a flooded local bridge as “breaking news” to get clicks.
3. **Classmate’s picture:** Uploading a classmate’s selfie to an AI cartoon filter and posting it online without asking.
4. **Original flyer illustration:** Generating an AI watercolor illustration of books for a community book-swap poster (no real faces, allowed by tool terms).
5. **Customer audio:** Uploading a recorded customer support call (with full customer name and address) to a public transcription site without approval.

#### Suggested Decisions
1. **Do not proceed** (voice cloning without consent; high impersonation risk).
2. **Do not proceed** (misleading deepfake / misinformation).
3. **Ask permission** (never use a real person’s likeness or upload their photo without consent).
4. **Proceed with label** (e.g., *“Illustration generated with AI”* + alt text).
5. **Do not proceed / Ask approval** (privacy breach—strip private data and use an approved tool).

---

### Stretch Task (Advanced Users)
Write a **one-page AI media policy** for a small team, club, or community group covering: *Consent, Labeling, Privacy, Ownership/Terms, and Review before publishing*.

lessons.title: 9.3 Module 9 Knowledge Check (10 Questions from 20-Question Bank)
lessons.summary: 10 questions randomly drawn from the 20-question Module 9 bank (15 minutes).

quiz_questions.question: Which five questions should you ask before using AI-generated media?
options: Who is shown/heard, did they agree, who owns/may use it, is it labeled, and could it mislead/harm?
Is it cheap, fast, loud, bright, and long?
quiz_questions.explanation: These five checks cover consent, rights, transparency, and harm.

quiz_questions.question: A friend wants to clone a teacher’s voice as a joke. What is the right decision?
options: Do not proceed—never clone or imitate a real person’s voice without explicit consent
Proceed if it is under 30 seconds
quiz_questions.explanation: Voice likeness requires explicit consent.

quiz_questions.question: Why should you take care when prompting “in the style of [living artist]”?
options: It raises ethical and copyright/ownership concerns around copying a living creator’s signature style
quiz_questions.explanation: Describe visual traits (palette, brushwork, mood) rather than mimicking living artists.

quiz_questions.question: What is “provenance” in AI media?
options: Labels, notes, or metadata showing where media came from and whether AI was used
quiz_questions.explanation: Provenance helps viewers verify origin and authenticity.

quiz_questions.question: True or false: Posting a realistic AI photo of a fake disaster as real news is harmful misinformation even if meant as a prank.
quiz_questions.explanation: Misleading synthetic media erodes trust and can cause real panic.

quiz_questions.question: What does “Label it, ask first” mean?
options: Disclose AI generation honestly and get permission before using someone’s likeness, voice, or private data
quiz_questions.explanation: Consent before creating and transparency when sharing prevent most harms.

quiz_questions.question: If an AI image generator repeatedly shows only one gender when you prompt “engineer” or “nurse,” what issue are you seeing?
options: Bias and stereotypes in generated media
quiz_questions.explanation: Review outputs for bias and specify diverse, fair representation.

quiz_questions.question: Before using an AI image in a commercial flyer, what should you check?
options: The tool’s terms of service on ownership and commercial rights
quiz_questions.explanation: Tool terms differ on free vs. paid commercial usage rights.

quiz_questions.question: True or false: Uploading a classmate’s photo to an AI editor without asking respects their privacy and likeness.
quiz_questions.explanation: Always ask permission before uploading someone else’s photo.

quiz_questions.question: Which label is clearest on a community poster with an AI illustration?
quiz_questions.explanation: Plain, honest disclosure is best.

quiz_questions.question: Why keep provenance metadata or watermarks intact when tools add them?
options: They help preserve transparency about how the media was made
quiz_questions.explanation: Preserving provenance supports media literacy.

quiz_questions.question: What should you do if a school or workplace forbids AI for a specific assignment?
options: Follow the rule and do not use AI on that assignment
Ask a friend to submit it
quiz_questions.explanation: Responsible use includes respecting local rules.

quiz_questions.question: True or false: Safety refusals in AI tools exist to block harmful content like impersonation or illegal acts.
quiz_questions.explanation: Guardrails help prevent obvious misuse, though human judgment is still needed.

quiz_questions.question: Why avoid uploading private recordings to unknown free audio tools?
options: Uploaded audio may be stored, reviewed, or used to train models depending on tool terms
Free tools delete everything in 1 millisecond
quiz_questions.explanation: Treat public tools as non-confidential unless approved.

quiz_questions.question: Which element belongs in a team’s one-page AI media policy?
options: Clear rules on consent, honest labeling, privacy, and human review before publishing
quiz_questions.explanation: Practical policies give teams clear, repeatable guardrails.

quiz_questions.question: If you edit a real photo heavily with AI so the scene looks totally different, should you disclose it?
options: Yes, especially if viewers might mistake it for an unedited documentary photo
Only if it is black and white
quiz_questions.explanation: Disclosing major synthetic edits prevents misleading viewers.

quiz_questions.question: True or false: Copyright and AI ownership rules are identical in every country.
quiz_questions.explanation: Rules differ by jurisdiction and change over time—check local guidance and tool terms.

quiz_questions.question: What is the best response when an AI tool generates a stereotyped image?
options: Do not use it; refine your prompt with specific, fair details and review again
quiz_questions.explanation: You control what you publish—refine and curate responsibly.

quiz_questions.question: Which case requires “Ask permission” first?
options: Using a colleague’s headshot in an AI-styled team avatar
quiz_questions.explanation: Using any real person’s face requires their consent.

quiz_questions.question: Who is accountable for misleading or harmful AI media once it is shared?
options: The person or organization who chose to generate and publish it
quiz_questions.explanation: Human publishers remain responsible for what they release.

sections.title: Part 3 — Module 10: Advanced Workflows and Prompt Systems (50 min)

lessons.title: 10.1 Lesson & Reading: Prompt Chains, Structured Output, Testing & “A Prompt Is Never Finished” (20 min)
lessons.summary: Design cross-media prompt chains, enforce spreadsheet-ready structured output, use reusable house-style instruction sets, test prompts on 5 varied inputs with a scorecard, and version/retire prompts.
lessons.content:
> **What you will learn:** Design multi-step workflows, build reusable instruction sets, and test prompts on varied inputs. *(12 min lesson + 8 min reading)*

---

### Part A: The Lesson (12 minutes)
1. **Prompt chains across media:** Connect steps cleanly—for example: *Research notes → 4-section outline → 60-second voice script → 4-shot video/image prompts*. Check each step before feeding the next.
2. **Structured output (no coding):** Ask for **fixed fields, pipe-delimited rows, or Markdown tables** with exact column names so outputs paste straight into a spreadsheet.
3. **Reusable instruction sets:** Save a short “house style” block (audience, reading level, forbidden words, preferred format) to paste at the start of any chat.
4. **Testing & scorecards:** Never trust a prompt after one lucky run. Test it on **5 varied inputs** (easy, short, messy, edge-case, ambiguous) and score each on a simple 1–3 scale (*Accuracy, Format compliance, Clarity*).
5. **Versioning, time/cost & when NOT to use AI:** Label templates `v1`, `v2`, `v3`. Skip AI when a 2-minute manual task is faster, or when high-stakes judgment/privacy makes AI unsafe.

---

### Part B: Reading (8 minutes) — “A Prompt Is Never Finished”
AI models and tools evolve constantly. A prompt that worked six months ago may become too wordy, miss new formatting rules, or fail on newer tasks. Schedule quick check-ins: **keep what works, update what drifts, and retire prompts that no longer earn their keep.**

lessons.title: 10.2 Activity: Design a Workflow & Stretch 5-Input Scorecard (15 min)
lessons.summary: Map a five-step cross-media workflow for a real mini-project (prompt, check, and risk at each step), plus a Stretch 5-input test set & scorecard.
lessons.content:
> **Your goal:** Map a **five-step workflow** for a real mini-project (for example: *a 1-minute community explainer video* or *a monthly newsletter*) in your **Personal Study Notes**. *(15 minutes)*

---

### Five-Step Workflow Table
For each of the 5 steps, fill in: **Step Goal | Prompt / Template | Human Check | Main Risk**
- *Example Step 1:* Gather & verify 3 facts → Check every source URL → Risk: hallucinated stat.
- *Example Step 2:* Outline 3 key points → Check audience fit → Risk: jargon.
- *Example Step 3:* Draft ear-ready script → Read aloud for timing → Risk: robotic phrasing.
- *Example Step 4:* Generate 2 supporting image prompts + alt text → Check visual bias/no text → Risk: cluttered image.
- *Example Step 5:* Final responsible-use & label check → Confirm consent & AI disclosure → Risk: missing label.

---

### Stretch Task (Advanced Users)
Build a **five-input test set** (easy, short, messy, edge-case, ambiguous) and a **simple scorecard** (e.g., *Format 0–2, Accuracy 0–2, Tone 0–2*) for one of your templates, run or trace all five, and report where it failed and what you changed.

lessons.title: 10.3 Module 10 Knowledge Check (10 Questions from 20-Question Bank)
lessons.summary: 10 questions randomly drawn from the 20-question Module 10 bank (15 minutes).

quiz_questions.question: Why test a reusable prompt template on five varied inputs instead of just one?
options: One easy run hides edge-case failures on messy, short, or ambiguous inputs
quiz_questions.explanation: Varied testing exposes brittle instructions before you depend on them.

quiz_questions.question: How can you get spreadsheet-ready output without writing code?
options: Ask for fixed field names or a Markdown table with exact column headers
Ask for a long story with no headings
quiz_questions.explanation: Consistent columns and delimiters paste cleanly into spreadsheets.

quiz_questions.question: What is a “house style” instruction set?
options: A reusable block of tone, audience, and format rules pasted at the start of chats
quiz_questions.explanation: House style blocks keep outputs consistent across sessions.

quiz_questions.question: Why put a human check between steps in a cross-media prompt chain?
options: So an error in Step 1 (like a wrong fact) does not poison Steps 2, 3, and 4
To slow things down for no reason
Because chains cannot have more than 1 step
quiz_questions.explanation: Catching errors early prevents wasted downstream work.

quiz_questions.question: What does “A prompt is never finished” mean?
options: As tools and your needs change, prompts should be reviewed, versioned, and retired when outdated
quiz_questions.explanation: Periodic maintenance keeps your prompt library reliable.

quiz_questions.question: When is it better NOT to use AI for a task?
options: When a quick manual edit is faster, or when privacy/high stakes make AI unsafe
Whenever a task takes under 1 hour
quiz_questions.explanation: Knowing when to skip AI saves time and reduces risk.
